Rules/Regulations and issues, relating to them along with the comments received from the 
Government. The observations and recommendations of the Committee are contained in 
the succeeding paragraphs of the Report. 
 
 
DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA  A. HEPTULLA 
Chairperson, 
Committee on Subordinate Legislation, 
Rajya Sabha 
NEW DELHI; 
18th February, 2009. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
REPORT 
I 
Amendment in the Schedule M of the Drug and Cosmetics  
( Eighth Amendment) Rules, 2001 
1.  The Committee was informed that the National Human Rights Commission 
(NHRC) in its investigation of certain complain ts relating to quality of Intravenous (I.V.) 
Fluids had in their order dated 31st March, 1999 made exclusive recommendations in 
respect of manufacture, distribution and storage of the drugs and the need to upgrade 
Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) given unde r Schedule M. In its submission before 
NHRC, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare had promised to revise the 
requirements of the GMPs under the Drug and Cosmetics Rules. It was also informed by 
the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare that World Health Organisation (WHO) had 
prescribed such guidelines for the member countries and that th e guidelines were 
periodically revised. The Ministry also  submitted that adherence to such Good 
Manufacturing Practices under Schedule M was essential for sustaining the export of 
drugs and pharmaceuticals to other countries. 
2.   The Committee was informed that th e Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 framed 
under the Sections 12 and 33 of the Drug and Cosmetics Act, 1940, needed to be 
amended. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare further informed the Committee 
that objections and suggestions from the public were invited for 45 days since the 5th 
January, 2001. Thereafter the Government in consultation with the Drugs Technical 
Advisory Board notified the amendments on the 11th December, 2001. The application of 
such amendments on licensed manufacturers was initially deferred till the 31st December, 
2003. 
3.   Rules 71, 74, 76 and 78 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules 1945 provided for 
Schedule M, which prescribed the ‘Good Manufacturing Practices and Requirements of 
Premises, Plant and Equipment for the Pharma ceutical Products’. The Amendment also 
required each licensee to evolve appropriate methodology, system and procedures which 
shall be used exclusively for the production of drugs and no other manufacturing activity 
were to be undertaken in the premises. It was informed by the Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare that the new amendments lay stress on: 
z Adequate documentation at every stage of production 
z  Validation of process and equipments 
z Efficient Standard Op erative Procedures (SOPs) at every stage of 
manufacture and quality control operations 
z Adequate and periodic training to the technical personnel in the industry 
4.   The Committee examined the amended Rules and the views of the Ministry were 
ascertained through a questionnaire and a subsequent meeting with the Secretary, 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Following issues were raised with the Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare: 

Issue I 
 If the revised Schedule M would be detrimental to the interests of the small 
scale manufacturers and may even lead to  large scale unemployment due to closure 
of such units. 
Ministry’s Reply 
 The revised Schedule M was not detrimental to the interests of small scale 
units and a large number of such units ha d already upgraded their facilities or were 
in process of doing so. 
Issue II 
 If the SSI sector as a whole or only a select associations were consulted on 
the subject. 
Ministry’s reply 
 All the sectors of pharmaceutical indust ry were consulted. Consultations were 
held with the Indian Drug Manufacturers’ Association (IDMA), which also has 
SSIs as its members. 
Issue III 
 If the apprehensions of the SSI units justified that application of revised 
Schedule M would require large investment in equipments, increase in area, large 
amount of documentation and validations that may further require increase in 
personnel. 
Ministry’s Reply 
 Eighty per cent of the Schedule M norms require proper application of norms 
and good practices and do not require any investment. Only 20% requires a change 
in infrastructure facilities. However, as per the representations from the industry 
some changes have been made in schedule like deletion of requirement for 
additional space. 
Issue IV 
 If the contention of SSI sector was genuine that the revised Schedule M were 
formulated by those with limited exposure only to big manufacturers. 
Ministry’s Reply 
 Inputs had been taken from the drug regulatory authorities of various States 
who were conversant with the status of  small scale industries in their respective 
States. Also the industry organizations li ke IDMA with sizable SSI membership 
were consulted. 
 
 
 
 
 

Issue V 
 What is the mechanism for monitoring the compliance of the revised 
Schedule M. 
Ministry’s Reply 
 States have begun to audit firms to ensure the compliance of the norms. The 
status of compliance varied from State to State. 
Issue VI 
 If the Government had any plan for the SSI sector in respect of 
implementation of revived Schedule M 
Ministry’s Reply 
 The Government had convened workshops in various parts of the country for 
educating the SSIs on Good Manufacturing Practices as prescribed in the revised 
Schedule M. The National Institute for Pharmaceutical Education and Research 
(NIPER) has also conducted training programmes for the production and analytical 
staff of the SSI units. 
Issue VII 
 The Licensing Authority has been given the discretionary powers to relax the 
provisions regarding nature and extent of manufacturing operations, equipments, 
areas etc. of the Schedule M. Whether such  discretionary power were likely to be 
misused. 
Ministry’s Reply 
 Such discretionary powers were available in earlier version of the Schedule 
M and such discretionary powers to the licensing authority have been given only for 
chemical and pharmaceutical aids, bandages, medical gases, empty gelatin capsules 
etc. for which the Schedule M does not prescribe specific requirements of space and 
equipments. 
Issue VIII 
 Which of the demands of the small scale manufacturers were accepted and 
what specific demands were found unacceptable. 
Ministry’s Reply 
 Demands of small scale manufacturers like use of alternative material instead 
of aluminum, removal of ancillary area, us age of non-linting cleaning material in 
the sterile area for cleaning etc. have been accepted. 
5.   The Committee also acknowledged th e observations made by the Department 
related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare in their 12th 
Report on the Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment) Bill, 2005, wherein the Committee has 
recommended stringent measures against ma nufacturing spurious and sub-standard 
medicines and drugs. 
6.   The Committee noted from the representation of All India Small Scale 
Pharmaceutical Manufacturers’ Association dated the 19th February, 2001 that it had 

objection over a few counts pertaining to disposal of waste, warehousing area, ancillary 
area and requirements of Plant and equipment which prescribed the minimum area 
required. The representation submitted that 
“The problem of specified area is in all the categories where you have enhanced the 
area for minimum requirement. Pharmaceu tical Units are mostly located in 
metropolitan cities and minimum area requi red for SSI sector will increase the 
cost.” 
  In this regard the Committee found distinct difference of opinion of the Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare and the Ministry  of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises 
(MSME). 
  The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare submitted that 
“The apprehensions expressed by the SSI are not realistic. On the average 80% of 
the Schedule M norms require change of mind set of technical persons and 
observance of good practices... This does not call for any investment but require 
good documentation. The rest 20% require ch ange in infrastructure facilities which 
may involve some financial investment.” 
  However, the Ministry of MSME has been more candid in this regard. It concurred 
with the apprehensions raised by the small scale manufacturers. It submitted in writing 
that: 
“It is indeed a fact that implementation of revised Schedule M norms involves 
additional infrastructural requirements in most cases. One of the major 
requirements is that of space mainly for additional equipments like air handling 
units etc. Since a large number of small scale pharma units are located in old 
industrial estates or congested localities in  cities, the scope of expansion of their 
existing premises is very limited. Relo cating in new premises will involve 
considerable expenditure.” 
7.   The Committee also took note of the is sues raised in the representations made by 
the associations of small scale drug manufactu rers and the Secretary, Ministry of Micro, 
Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) pertaini ng to difficulty faced by the small scale 
manufacturers in abiding the timeline. It also observed that the Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare had tried to accommodate the requests made by the industry associations 
in this regard and the last date for compliance had been repeatedly extended upto the 30th 
June, 2005. However grievances from sm all scale manufacturers regarding the 
cancellation or non renewal of licenses on the grounds of non-compliance of Schedule M 
still remain unaddressed. The Ministry of MSME informed the Committee that its request 
on behalf of Confederation of Indian Pharma  Industry (CIPI) for another extension was 
not conceded by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. 
8.   The Committee also took cognizance of the complaints of closure of certain small 
scale pharma units in certain States. Upon th e query regarding the extent of such cases of 
closure due to non-compliance of Schedule M, the representative of the Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare submitted before the Committee – 

“It is very difficult to tell. We have already sent a communication to the State 
authorities and we are getting feedback from  them. We are in process of collecting 
the feedback. There are substantial numbers of units which have already adopted 
the revised norms. There are substantial number of units which are serious about 
it.” 
9.   The Committee was informed that the Ministry of MSME had a continuing Credit 
Linked Capital Subsidy scheme for the modernisation and technology upgradation in the 
small scale sector and that the Department of Chemical too had proposed a scheme for the 
Planning Commission’s approval whereby 5% intere st subsidy were to be provided on an 
amount up to Rs. one crore. 
10.   The Committee was also cognizant of the enabling provisions of new MSME 
Development Act, 2006. The Act has enhanced the investment limit in plant and 
machinery upto Rs.5 crores for small scale units and Rs. 5-10 crores for medium scale 
units. The Act also provides for the proc urement preference policy wherein the 
Government Ministries/Departments, aided ins titutions and Public Sector Units will be 
required to procure goods produced by micr o and small units. Further the MSME Act, 
2006 also provides for the creation of Funds where the Grants from the Government for a 
specific purpose could be credited. 
11.   The Committee is in agreement with  the amendments proposed in the 
Schedule M of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, which it feels will ensure 
adherence to the good manufacturing practices and requirements of premises, plants 
and equipment for the pharmaceutical products by the manufacturers. Not only 
these amendments are in sync with the stated objective to make the country an 
international hub in drug and pharmaceutical manufacturing, but such standards 
are also desirable to protect the inte rests of consumers. The Committee also 
acknowledges that the Ministry of Health  and Family Welfare had undertaken an 
elaborate consultative process with the indus try experts, representative associations 
and had given 45-days window for the stakeholders to submit their views and 
comments on the proposed amendments an d that the timeline was extended till 30th 
June, 2005. The Committee concurs with th e concerns expressed by the Secretary, 
Ministry of MSME during his evidence before  it that despite some of their concerns 
being accommodated, the small scale manufa cturers find it difficult to meet the 
deadline. Further, compliance with the am endments will require significant capital 
investment. 
12.   The Committee recommends that the G overnment should proactively reach 
out to the SSIs in pharma sector to support them during the transitory phase as they 
graduate to become Schedule M compli ant. Government should promote the 
Schemes like Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS) and Credit 
Guarantee Fund Scheme among the small sc ale drug manufacturers to enable them 
to access the institutional credit. 
13.   Under the amended Schedule M, the manufacturers are expected to evolve 
appropriate methodology, systems and procedures which should be documented and 
maintained fo r inspection and reference. The Committee recommends that the 

coverage of Certification Reimbursement Sc heme should be extended to cover the 
expenditure incurred by the small sc ale manufacturers in maintaining the 
documentation. Also special package for the small scale pharma units should be 
made under the Micro and Sm all Enterprise Cluster Development Programnme, so 
that, such Units could avail the integrated infrastructure facilities. 
14.   The Committee takes note that the Department of Chemical had submitted a 
proposal with the Planning Commission to provide 5% interest subsidy on the credit 
upto Rs. 1 crore. The Committee suggests that  the in addition to interest subsidy the 
said scheme should be linked with the Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme to 
provide upfront relief in capital investment. The Committee recommends to expedite 
this policy for early implementation. 
15.   The Committee takes cognizance  of the apprehen sions regarding 
interpretation and enforcement of provisions by the relevant authority. Considering 
that there remains a possibility of mis-interpretation of provisions during initial 
years of any rule/regulation, the Committee considers it an imperative that Ministry 
of Micro, Small and Medium Enterp rises should involve NIPER and the 
representative SSI organizations under its Entrepreneurship and Business 
Development Programmes to conduct work shops for the field level enforcement 
agencies of the Government and the technical personnel of such small 
manufacturing units. Such workshops will help the stakeholders  to interact and 
understand the functional constraints in implementing the amended provisions. 
16.   The Committee expresses its serious di sapproval over inexplicable delay in 
framing the rules pertaining to establishm ent of Funds as provided in the Micro, 
Small and Medium Enterprises Act,2 006. The Committee recommends that the 
Government should without any further de lay finalise rules for setting up such 
Funds specially to support the small scale drug manufacturers to meet the 
requirements prescribed in the amended Schedule M. 
17.   Also the Committee finds it unacceptabl e that rules and policies under the 
enabling provisions contained in the said Act have not been finalized. The Section 11 
of the Act provides for Procurement Preference Policy by the Central Government 
Ministries/Departments, aided institutions and PSUs in favour of goods and services 
produced by small and micro units. Howeve r, such policy has not been formulated 
as yet. The Committee noted that in absence of such policy, the Government 
Departments, institutions and PSUs have been imposing unreasonable 
conditionalities for placing orders of su pply. The Committee recommends that the 
Government must expedite the formulation of Purchase Preference Policy to remove 
handicaps faced by the small scale units in getting Government orders. 
18.   However, the Committee takes a very seri ous view of instances of closure of 
small scale units in certain States. The Committee takes into cognizance the concerns 
raised by the small drug manufacturers over the possibility that the proposed 
amendments were likely to favour the big manufacturers and the MNCs and deny 
the smaller units the level-playing field even in the domestic market. The Committee 
also notes the significant contribution of the small manufacturers in the annual 
medicine production. The Committee recogniz es that the presence of small scale 

sector in pharmaceutical industry is vital to bring about competition in this sector 
and to restrain the possible monopoly of few companies. In this respect the 
Committee found it conspicuous that two concerned Ministries i.e. Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare and the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises had different views over the impact of amended Schedule M on the SSIs 
in pharma sector. The Committee therefor e recommends that the Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises Development Organisation alongwith the Drug Technical 
Advisory Board should conduct a survey to ascertain the extent of cases of closure of 
SSIs in pharma sector due to non-complian ce of revised Schedule M ever since it 
became applicable from 1st July 2005. 
19.  The Committee has noted with concern the rising prices of drugs after the 
introduction of MRP base d excise regime. The regime has benefited certain 
companies who have either se t up their units in Exci se Free Zones or have 
contracted the production to units in such Excise Free Zones. This has defeated the 
entire purpose of introducing the MRP based excise regime to increase the revenue 
and has also denied the small scale manu facturers the level-playing field. The 
Committee is informed that the issue has been  considered at the highest levels in the 
Government, yet the anomaly remains. The Committee recommends that 
Government must dispel such impressi on. The Government must restore level-
playing field in the pharmaceutical and drug  manufacturing sector by rationalizing 
the fiscal incentives to avoid any misuse to skew the competition. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

II 
The State Bank of Mysore Officers’ Service  
Regulations, 1979––Implementation of 128th Report of the  
Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Rajya Sabha 
  The State Bank of Mysore Officers’ Se rvice Regulations, 19 79 was examined and 
the Committee in its 128th Report, which was presented to the House on the 14th March, 
2000 recommended as follows: 
The Committee during the course of the discussion at Mumbai did not agree 
with the replies of the State Bank of Mysore on definition of the word 
‘perquisite’, regulation 19 (1), and 38. The Committee desired that these 
regulations should be amended as per the suggestions of the Committee on the 
lines of similar regulations of the State Bank of India. The Committee, 
however, reviewed its earlier suggestions on regulations 3 (h), 15 (3), 16 (1) and 
36 and noted the comments of the Bank. As regards regulation 36, the 
Committee felt that the Ministry of Finance/Bank should find out the 
feasibility to rationalize th e provisions relating to maternity leave as per the 
provisions available in the Central Government Rules (Para 5). 
The Committee discussed the subject at its meeting held on March 1, 2000. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Finance/The State Bank of 
Mysore should take immediate steps to amend regulations 3 (definition of the 
word perquisites), 19 (1),38 as desired by it (Para 6). 
2.   Relevant extracts from the report were forwarded to the Ministry of Finance 
(Banking Division) on the 16th March, 2000 for necessary action. 
3.   The Ministry vide their communication dated the 23rd October, 2000 furnished the 
Action Taken Report. The Committee’s recommendation and the Ministry’s Action 
Taken Note is as under:–– 
(i) Regulation 3  
 The Committee desired that the term  “perquisites” may be defined in 
Regulation 3 entitled ‘Definitions’. 
Action Taken 
 The recommendation has been accepted  and State Bank of India has been 
advised to define the term “Perquisites” in the Regulation 3 of Officers Service 
Regulation of its Associate Banks. 
(ii) Regulation 19 (1)  
 The words “at its discretion” and “at the discretion of the executive 
committee” respectively appearing in the fi rst and third proviso be substituted with 
“for reason to be recorded in writing.” 
Action Taken 

 The recommendation made by the Committee has been accepted and State 
Bank of India has been advised to make necessary amendments in the Service 
Regulations of Associate Banks. 
(iii) Regulation 38  
 Upon a plain reading of Regulation 38 the confusion still remains inspite of 
the Bank’s reply to the questionnaire. Why not redraft this provision as per the 
discussions with nationalized banks, IBA and Ministry of Finance. 
Action Taken 
 The recommendation has been accepted  and State Bank of India has been 
advised to make modifications in Service Regulations of Associate Banks on the 
same lines as has been done by nationalized banks. 
(iii) Regulation 36: Maternity Leave  
 The Committee felt that the Ministry of Finance/banks should find out the 
feasibility to rationalise the provisions relating to Maternity Leave as per the 
provisions available in the Central Government rules. 
Action Taken 
 The service conditions in banks are broadly determined in pursuance of 
Bipartite Settlements/Understandings signed/reached by the workmen 
unions/officers associations with Indi an Banks’ Association (representing the 
Banks Managements). Hence, the same may not be exactly in conformity with the 
provisions applicable to Central Government employees. In the recent Bipartite 
Settlement Indian Banks Association had with the workmen unions, the provision 
for Maternity Leave has been modified . A statement indicating for existing 
provisions with regard to Maternity Leave in the Government and existing 
provisions in banks and the modi fied provisions is placed at Annexure-I. The 
question of modifying Officer Service Regulations on the same lines for bank 
officers are under consideration of Indian Banks’ Association. 
4.   The Ministry have since notified the amendments to Regulations 3 and 38 vide their 
notification SBD No.2/2002 dated the 11th February, 2002 (Annexure-II) and 
notification SBD No. 5/2002 dated the 25th May, 2002 (Annexure-III) respectively, as 
per the recommendations of the Committee. 
5.   However, further clarification was sought from the Ministry on the notification 
pertaining to amendment to State Bank of Mysore (Officers’) Service Regulations, 1979. 
The point referred to the Ministry and the comments/clarifications received thereon are 
reproduced below: 
 
Point referred 
 Regarding proper format in so far as the requirements of mentioning the 
G.S.R. No./S.O. No.; short title and date of commencement is concerned. 

Ministry’s comments (24th July, 2002) 
 The matter has been examined in consultation with State Bank of India. The 
Bank has reported that instead of G.S.R. or  S.O. No., they, as per past practice, are 
numbering all their notifications for publication in Gazette of India, as SBD No. for 
example SBD No. 5/2002. While SBD repres ents the name of their department viz. 
Subsidiary Banks Department, 5/2002 indicat es that the said notification was the 
5th Notification of the year 2002. The Bank has further reported that the different 
banks/institutions are following different practices and prefixing their notifications 
differently in the Gazette of India. As regards the short title and the date of 
commencement, the bank has reported that most of the amendments to the Service 
Regulations are carried out as per advise s of Indian Banks’ Association (IBA) and 
no change is made at their end. Similarl y, the title and date of commencement of 
their amendment to Regulation 38, is as per advice received from IBA. Incidentally, 
Regulation 38 has been further amended as per IBA advises and since been 
published in the Gazette of India dated 25th May, 2002 vide their notification SBD 
No. 5/2002. 
 Regarding amendment to Regulation 19 (1), the Ministry informed that the 
same is being examined by the Bank, and, Rajya Sabha S ecretariat, will be 
informed in the matter as soon as the amendment is finalized. 
6.  The Ministry on the 18th October, 2004 informed as under:- 
“Regulation 19 of the Officers’ Service Regulation is common to all State Bank 
of India group banks and amendment to Regulation 19 of the State Bank of 
Mysore (Officers’) Service Regulations,  1979 can be carried out only after 
similar amendment is made in the service rules of State Bank of India”. 
  The Ministry, accordingly, requested for extension of time up to the 31st December, 
2004 for carrying out the amendments which was acceded to. 
7.   The Ministry vide their communications dated the 21st February, 2005, the 22nd 
March, 2006, the 28th June, 2006 and the 25th October, 2006 had repeatedly sought 
extension of time for finalization/notification of the amendment to regulation 19(1) but it 
was not done so during the extended period. 
8.   The Ministry in its last communication to the Ministry on the 26th September, 2008 
while furnishing a status note on the subject stated thus: 
 “The SBI Officers Service Rules are ma de by the Central Board of the State 
Bank of India in terms of the powers conf erred by sub section (1) of Section 43 of 
the State Bank of India Act, 1955. Similarly, the Associate Banks Officers Service 
Regulations, 1979 are framed by the Central Board of Directors of SBI in 
consultation with the Board of the Directors of the Associate Banks with the 
previous approval of RBI in terms of powers conferred by Section 63 of the SBI 
(Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959. 
 Keeping the above provisions of the Act in view, SBI has been advised to 
revisit the matter in the light of the recommendations of the Committee.” 

9.   The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry of Finance (Department of 
Financial Services) has carried out amendments in Regulations 3 and 38 of the State 
Bank of Mysore Officers’ Service Regulati ons, 1979, as recommended by it. The 
Committee however takes a serious view on  the inordinate delay in carrying out 
amendments to Regulation 19(1). The Committee notes the fact that Regulation 19 of 
the Officers’ Service Regulation is common to all State Bank of India group banks 
and amendment to Regulation 19 of the State Bank of Mysore Officers’ Service 
Regulations, 1979 can be carried out only after similar amendment is made in the 
service rules of State Bank of India. Th e Committee expresses its dismay over the 
fact that despite its reiteration desired amendments to Regulation 19(1) which is 
adversely affecting the interest of the offi cers of the State Bank of Mysore could not 
be carried out. The Committee is also surp rised that the Ministry has not yet given 
any explanation regarding non-acceptance of the Committee’s recommendation. By 
simply delaying the process, the Ministry  has put the career of these officers in 
doldrums. The Committee is of the opinion that there should be uniformity in the 
service regulations of SBI and its associate banks as this will also help in 
smoothening the proposed merger with its associate banks. The Committee therefore 
reiterates its earlier st and regarding amendment to Regulation 19(1) and 
recommends that the Ministry should carry out the amendment expeditiously, under 
intimation to it.

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS 
Amendment in the Schedule M of the Dr ug and Cosmetics (Eighth Amendment) 
Rules, 2001 
  The Committee is in agreement with  the amendments proposed in the 
Schedule M of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules 1945, which it feels will ensure 
adherence to the good manufacturing practices and requirements of premises, plants 
and equipment for the pharmaceutical products by the manufacturers. Not only 
these amendments are in sync with the stated objective to make the country an 
international hub in drug and pharmaceutical manufacturing, but such standards 
are also desirable to protect the inte rests of consumers. The Committee also 
acknowledges that the Ministry of Health and family Welfare had undertaken an 
elaborate consultative process with the indus try experts, representative associations 
and had given 45-days window for the stakeholders to submit their views and 
comments on the proposed amendments and that the timeline was extended till 30 
June 2005. The Committee concurs with the concerns expressed by the Secretary, 
Ministry of MSME during his evidence before  it that despite some of their concerns 
being accommodated, the small scale manufa cturers find it difficult to meet the 
deadline. Further, compliance with the am endments will require significant capital 
investment. (Para 11) 
  The Committee recommends that the G overnment should proactively reach 
out to the SSIs in pharma sector to supp ort during the transitory phase as they 
graduate to become Schedule M compliant. Government should promote the 
Schemes like Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS) and Credit 
Guarantee Fund Scheme among the small sc ale drug manufacturers to enable them 
to access the institutional credit. ( Para 12) 
  Under the amended Schedule M, the manufacturers are expected to evolve 
appropriate methodology, systems and procedures which should be documented and 
maintained fo r inspection and reference. The Committee recommends that the 
coverage of Certification Reimbursement Sc heme should be extended to cover the 
expenditure incurred by the small sc ale manufacturers in maintaining the 
documentation. Also special package for the small scale pharma units should be 
made under the Micro and Sm all Enterprise Cluster Development Programnme, so 
that, such Units could avail the integrated infrastructure facilities.    ( Para 13) 
  The Committee takes note that the Department of Chemical had submitted a 
proposal with the Planning Commission to provide 5% interest subsidy on the credit 
upto Rs 1 crore. The Committee suggests that the in addition to interest subsidy the 
said scheme should be linked with the Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme to 
provide upfront relief in capita investment. The Committee recommends to expedite 
the policy for early implementation. (Para 14) 
  The Committee takes cognizance of the apprehen sions regarding 
interpretation and enforcement of provisions by the relevant authority. Considering 

that there remains a possibility of mis-interpretation of provisions during initial 
years of any rule/regulation, the Committee considers it an imperative that Ministry 
of Micro, Small and Medium Enterp rises should involve NIPER and the 
representative SSI organizations under its Entrepreneurship and Business 
Development Programmes to conduct work shops for the field level enforcement 
agencies of the Government and the technical personnel of such small 
manufacturing units. Such workshops will help the stakeholders  to interact and 
understand the functional constraints in implementing the amended provisions.
(Para 15) 
  The Committee expresses its serious di sapproval over inexplicable delay in 
framing the rules pertaining to establishm ent of Funds as provided in the Micro, 
Small and Medium Enterprises Act,2 006. The Committee recommends that the 
Government should without any further de lay finalise rules for setting up such 
Funds specially to support the small scale drug manufacturers to meet the 
requirements prescribed in the amended Schedule M.      ( Para 16) 
  Also the Committee finds it unacceptable that rules and policies under the 
enabling provisions contained in the said Act have not been finalized. The Section 11 
of the Act provides for Procurement Preference Policy by the Central Government 
Ministries/Departments, aided institutions and PSUs in favour of goods and services 
produced by small and micro units. However such Policy has not been formulated as 
yet. The Committee noted that in abse nce of such policy the Government 
Departments, institutions and PSU have been imposing unreasonable 
conditionalities for placing orders of su pply. The Committee recommends that the 
Government must expedite the formulation of Purchase Preference Policy to remove 
handicaps faced by the Small scale units in getting Government orders.(Para 17) 
  However, the Committee takes a very se rious view of instances of closure of 
small scale units in certain States. The Committee takes into cognizance the concerns 
raised by the small drug manufacturers over the possibility that the proposed 
amendments were likely to favour the big manufacturers and the MNCs and deny 
the smaller units the level-playing field even in the domestic market. The Committee 
also notes the significant contribution of the small manufacturers in the annual 
medicine production. The Co mmittee recognizes that the presence of small scale 
sector in pharmaceutical industry is vital to bring about competition in this sector 
and to restrain the possible monopoly of few companies. In this respect the 
Committee found it conspicuous that two concerned Ministries  i.e.  Ministry of 
Health and Family welfare and the Ministry of MSME had different views over the 
impact of amended Schedule M on the SSIs in pharma sector. The Committee 
therefore recommends that the MSME De velopment Organisation alongwith the 
Drug Technical Advisory Board should con duct a survey to ascertain the extent of 
cases of closure of SSIs in pharma sector due to non-compliance of revised Schedule 
M ever since it became applicable from 1st July 2005. (Para 18) 
  The Committee has noted with concern the rising prices of drugs after the 
introduction of MRP base d excise regime. The regime has benefited certain 
companies who have either se t up their units in Exci se Free Zones or have 

contracted the production to units in such Excise Free Zones. This has defeated the 
entire purpose of introducing the MRP based excise regime to increase the revenue 
and has also denied the small scale manu facturers the level-playing field. The 
Committee is informed that the issue has been  considered at the highest levels in the 
Government, yet the anomaly remains. The Committee recommends that 
Government must dispel such impressi on. The Government must restore level-
playing field in the pharmaceutical and drug  manufacturing sector by rationalizing 
the fiscal incentives to avoid any misuse to skew the competition.       (Para 19)

indicates the period of dela y in cases where notifications  have not been laid as 
per the schedule prescribed by the Committee and where such notifications 
were accompanied by a statement indicating the reasons for the delay in laying. 
In some of the cases the delay has been quite long. The 
observations/recommendations of the Co mmittee in respect of the specific 
Ministries/Departments are as follows: -    
  
(i) Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Agriculture & 
Cooperation) 
  
 The Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Agriculture & 
Cooperation) have laid 7 no tifications out of which 2 (Sl. Nos. 1 to 2) have 
been delayed. Out of those none of th e  delayed notifications have been 
accompanied by any delay statements. The delay ranges from 1 year 5 months 
to 1 year 10 months.  
 
  

: 3 : 
 
 The Committee notes with regret that  the Ministry of Agriculture 
have made inordinate delays in laying  of notifications as set out by the 
Committee in its recommendations. There is no delay statement appended 
to know why such delay has occurred . The Committee impresses upon the 
Ministry to ensure timely laying of notifications and where there is delay, 
delay statements should invariably be appended therewith. 
 
(ii) (Ministry of Civil Aviation)  
 
The Ministry of Civil Aviation have laid five notifications out of which 
one notification has been delayed.  Th e delay period extend s upto 1 year and 
one month.  There is no delay statement  appended either. 
 
 The Committee expresses its concern over such inordinate delay in 
laying of notification a nd urges upon the Ministry of  Civil Aviation to 
avoid extreme delays. A de lay statement should invariably be appended 
where laying of subordinate legislation is delayed. 
 
(iii) Ministry of Communicati on and Information Technology 
 
 (Department of Telecommunication) 
 
Department of Telecommunication ha ve laid 2 notifications one of 
which has been delayed. The delay ra nges upto five months and no delay 
statement have been attached. 
 
The Committee impresses upon the Ministry of Communication 
and Information Technology (Department of Telecommunications) to 
evolve suitable mechanism to avoid su ch delays and also to append delay 
statements where there has been a delay, in laying of the notifications. 
 
(iv) Ministry of Consumer Affairs,  Food and Public Distribution  
 
(Department of Consumer Affairs)  
 
Department of Consumer Affairs have  laid five notifications four of 
which have been delayed. The delay period ranged from four to five months.  
There is no delay statement  appended with the delayed notifications. 
 
 The Committee reiterates its recommendation that in case of delay 
in laying, notifications should be a ccompanied by a  delay statement. The 
Ministry should take care that repet ition of such delay is avoided in 
future.  
 

: 4 : 
 
(v) Ministry of Corporate Affairs 
 
  Ministry of Corporate Affairs have laid 11 notifications out of which  4 
notifications  have been delayed by two to three months. These have been 
accompanied with delay statements. The reason for delay given by the 
Ministry is as under:- 
 
 “The notifications could not be laid before both the Houses of 
Parliament within the prescribed period as while the Ministry was in process of 
authenticating and laying the notification in both the Houses of Parliament it 
was adjourned sine die before its due date of adjournment.” 
 
  The Committee observes that sessions are declared much in 
advance and had the Ministry of Corp orate Affairs taken prompt steps 
for laying of the notifications, th e delay could have been avoided. It 
appears to have wanted till last  movement. The Committee recommends 
that the Ministry should take the fi rst available opportunity for laying of 
their notifications during the session. 
 
(vi)  Ministry of Defence 
 
  The only notification that the Ministry  of Defence have laid has been 
delayed by seven months without any delay statement being appended 
therewith. 
 
  The Committee emphasizes that the Mi nistry should take steps to 
avoid delay in laying of notifications and where there is delay the 
notifications should be accompanied by delay statement/explaining the 
reasons therefore. 
 
(vii) Ministry of Finance 
 
 (Department of Economic Affairs) 
 
 The Ministry of Finance (Departmen t of Economic Affairs) have laid 8 
notifications out of which  2 notifications have not been laid within time. There 
has been a delay of four to five mont hs in laying of notifications. No delay 
statement is appended with either of these notifications. 
  
 The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Finance 
(Department of Economic Affairs) should evolve an effective mechanism 
to obviate possibility of such delays and in case of delay in laying of 
notifications, delay statements should invariably be attached with them.

 (viii)-A       Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services) 
  
 The Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services) have laid 3 
notifications out of which  one notifica tion have been delayed by five months.

 The Committee desires that the Mi nistry of Finance (Department 
of Financial Services) wo uld take action accordingly, in order to comply 
with the prescribed schedule in the matter of laying of Statutory 
Notifications. 
  
(viii)-B       Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) 
 
 The Ministry of Finance (Departm ent of Revenue) have laid 66 
notifications and 4 of them have been delayed, with delay of 4 months to 1

notifications and two notifications have been accompanied with delay 
statements. The reasons given by the Mini stry for delayed  notifications that 
the Ministry is involved in the Budget making exercise relating to the Direct 
Taxes. 
  
 Though the Ministry of Finan ce appended delay statements with 
two notifications, rest two other notifications were laid without and 
proper delay statements which w ere delayed for 4 and 5 months 
respectively. The  Committee  feels that though the delay period is 
negligible even then Ministry should invariably append the delay 
statement. However, the Committee is happy to note that the Ministry of 
Finance has appended delay statement with 62 notifications and the 
reasons given therein one quite convincing.

 The Department of Health have la id 10 notifications out of which 7

Department of Ayurveda, Yoga, Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha,

The Ministry of Home Affairs have laid 16 notifications. 3 of these 
have been delayed. The delay period ranges from 7 months to 1 year & 3 
month. All 3 notifications have been attached with delay statement. The 
reasons for delay given is as under:- 
 
The Notification G.S.R. 228 (E) and G.S.R. 255 (E) were published in 
the Gazette of India (Extraordinary) Part -II, Section 3(i). The rules could not 
be laid down before each House of Parl iament in the Budget Session due to 
adjournment of both the Houses. 
 
 The Committee recommends that Mi nistry should take the first 
available opportunity for laying the st atutory Notifications and, should 
not postpone this work for the later part of the session so that the 
eventualities like early prorogation of the House, which is of course rare, 
could be avoided.

 The Directorate General of Empl oyment and Training have laid 3

th Report, wherein it is laid down that it is essential to append a

appended delay statement in case of any delay.

expiry of the Session immediately following the said Session. All the 
Ministries/Departments of Governme nt of India should henceforth 
comply with this schedule in the matt er of laying of the Orders issued 
under various Acts of Parliament on the Table of the Rajya Sabha.

Report on 
The Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006  
Originally introduced in 1995, the Banking Ombudsma n Scheme enables speedy and 
cost effective resolution of complaints of bank cus tomers relating to deficiency in 
bank services. The Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006 ( Annexure I ) was framed by 
the Reserve Bank of India in exercise of power conf erred by Section 35A of  the 
Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The Scheme was introd uced with the object of 
enabling resolution of complaints relating to certain services rendered by banks and to 
facilitate the satisfaction or settlement of such complaints. The Reserve Bank of India 
is mandated to ensure that all commercial banks, pr ivate banks, regional rural banks, 
and scheduled primary co-operative banks shall comp ly with the Banking 
Ombudsman Scheme, 2006.  The Scheme provides appoin tment of Chief General 
Manager or General Manager of the RBI as Banking  O mbudsmen to be located at 
places identified by the it. Chapter III of the Sch eme defines jurisdiction, powers and 
duties of Banking Ombudsmen. Chapter IV prescribes the procedure for redressal of 
grievances, grounds of complaints, settlement of co mplaints by agreement or award 
by the Banking Ombudsman. The Chapter also gives th e grounds of rejection of 
complaints and appeal against the award given by Ba nking Ombudsman before the 
Appellate Authority.    
1.  The customers can also now complain to the Banking Ombudsman against deficiency 
in almost any banking services (Annexure-II), including credit cards, after 
exhausting the channel available with the bank conc erned for resolving their 
complaints. The Banking Ombudsman tries to resolve the complaint through 
conciliation or mediation and even passes an award if it is not resolved through such 
settlement.   
2.  It was taken up for detailed examination by the Com mittee on Subordinate 
Legislation, Rajya Sabha due to the importance of t he Scheme for general public,. 
Under the Scheme, Ombudsman offices are set up at 1 5 places in different parts of 
country mainly in the State capitals ( Annexure III). Any  person who has grievance 
against a bank on any of the grounds listed in the Scheme can lodge a complaint to 

the Banking Ombudsman (BO) within whose jurisdictio n the branch or the office of 
the bank complained against is located. If the comp lainant is not satisfied with the 
award given by the BO, he can approach the Appellat e Authority for the redressal of 
his grievances.  
3.  The Scheme was further amended in May 2007 (Annexure IV). The Reserve Bank of 
India amended the Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006 to  enable the customers to 
appeal against the Banking Ombudsman's decision. Be fore the scheme was amended, 
the bank customers could appeal only against the aw ards given by the Banking 
Ombudsman. The appellate authority for the Banking Ombudsman Scheme is the 
Deputy Governor of Reserve Bank of India.

4.  The Committee observed that the eligibility, appoin tment and tenure of the 
Appellate Authority has not been given in the Scheme. Only the definitions given 
under Clause 3 (2) of Chapter I states that Appella te Authority meant the 
Deputy Governor in charge of the Department of Rese rve Bank implementing 
the Scheme. The Committee considers the appointment  of Appellate Authority 
was a substantive enabling provision and feels that  it should have been clearly 
mentioned as a separate Clause in Chapter IV instea d of   being included in the 
definitions. The Committee finds such omission unfortunate.  
5.  The Scheme was examined and a questionnaire on the subject was referred to the 
Ministry of  Finance (Department of Economic Affairs) for their 
comments/clarifications on 2 nd  February, 2007. The response of the Ministry was 
received. ( Annexure V ). 
6.  During the course of its examination the Committee has had discussions on the said 
Scheme with the representatives of the following pu blic sector as well as major 
private banks along with the Ministry of Finance as follows: 
 
 
7.  During the Committee interactions with the represen tatives of Allahabad Bank, 
UCo Bank and Union Bank of India at Kolkata on 7-8 June 2007, the 
representatives of these Banks appreciated the Sche me as an improvement over 
previous mechanism as it provided for appellate mec hanism as against 
reviewing authority previously. The current scheme gives the right to appeal to 
both Bank as well as the customer, whereas in the e arlier mechanism only the 
Bank had the right to seek a review (Annexure VI).   
8.  The Committee during its interactions with Oriental  Bank of Commerce and 
Punjab National Bank enquired about the performance  of lendings under 
Government schemes and the redressal of complaints by potential beneficiaries.

The representatives of Banks informed that the loan s were being disbursed as 
per the framework and the guidelines. The CMD of th e Oriental Bank of 
Commerce informed that mechanism was evolved to reg ister complaints 
through telephone and Internet and that the trainee  officers were being 
sensitized towards customers’ complaints . ( Annexure VII)     
9.    During the Committee’s interactions with Private banks at Mumbai in January 
2008, the representatives of the Private banks appr eciated the Scheme as cost 
affective expeditious mechanism for grievance redre ssal. The representatives of 
Axis bank, ICICI Bank, Deutsche Bank and HDFC Bank informed the 
Committee that the Scheme has prompted these banks to streamline the in-house 
grievance redressal mechanism at Brach level which is periodically inspected by 
the senior Bank officers. ( Annexure VIII)   
10.  The Ministry of Finance (Department of Economic Aff airs) on 24 th  July, 2007  
forwarded the views of Reserve Bank of India on the  following two specific 
issues related to the Banking Ombudsman Scheme : 
 
(i)  Reasons for not appointing senior officers from scheduled commercial 
banks who are well-versed with operations of bankin g industry as Banking 
Ombudsman . 
 
The issue was examined during the recent revision o f the Banking Ombudsman 
Scheme. It was considered that as the Banking Ombudsman received complaints 
against various banks for the deficiency in banking  services, appointing serving 
senior officer from the banking sector may create a conflict of interest. 
 
Further, the Banking Ombudsmen appointed in recent past are senior officers 
(in the rank of General Manager/Chief General Manag er) with an experience of 
around 20 to 25 years in supervision/regulatory dep artments in Reserve Bank. 
The arrangement is working satisfactorily and there are no complaints regarding 
role/functioning of the Banking Ombudsman from any quarter. 
 

Under the Banking Ombudsman Scheme 2006, RBI office rs with 20 years 
working experience and having exposure to banking o perations and supervision 
are posted as Banking Ombudsman.  The experience is  that considerable 
advantage arises out of such appointments as such o fficers are able to resolve 
complaints through mediation more efficiently as ba nks against whom the 
complaints are made view this as intervention by th e regulator and usually 
redress the grievance . 
 
(ii) Rationale behind having Banking Ombudsman and Appellate Authority 
from same organization . 
 
The Banking Ombudsman Scheme is formulated, monitored, run and supervised 
by Reserve Bank since its inception in 1995. The Ba nking Ombudsman is 
treated as a separate and independent entity from R eserve Bank and there is no 
interference from Reserve Bank in the decision maki ng process by Banking 
Ombudsmen in the individual cases. Reserve Bank’s r ole is restricted to 
issuance of guidelines on the running of the scheme. 
 
Further, the Appellate Authority is Deputy Governor  of Reserve Bank. 
Whenever an appeal is filed with the Appellate Auth ority, complete position of 
the complaint is seen. The decision of the Appellat e Authority is generally 
arrived at after taking the views of the complainant, bank, Banking Ombudsman 
and that of the Legal Department of the Reserve Ban k. It is, therefore, opined 
that having Banking Ombudsman and Appellate Authori ty from Reserve Bank 
itself is fully logical and justified. 
 
11.  Various suggestions that have come up before the Co mmittee and the comments 
of the RBI are given below: 
 
 (A) Pendency of cases is one area of concern.  Dis posal of cases was time 
consuming as response from banks was not prompt. 
 

Every effort is being made to reduce pending cases.   While it is possible to close 
cases earlier, attempt is made to ensure grievance redressal through persistent efforts 
which may require keeping a case pending for longer time.  Of the total complaints of 
nearly 45,000 dealt with in 2006-07, only 4% of com plaints were pending for more 
than 3 months (see the table below):

From the table above it can be seen that the pendin g cases of complaints are 
growing. Out of 44766 cases dealt with during 2006- 07, only 21662 cases were 
settled and 15914 cases could not be considered. The Committee does not agree 
with the reply of the RBI over the pendency and not es with deep anguish that 
the Ombudsman infrastructure is not adequate and re commends to the 
Government to improve the situation at the earliest. 
 
(B) Rejection of complaints is another major concer n with about 49% of complaints 
rejected. 
 
The actual percentage of complaints that were rejected was much lower as a sample 
study of the rejected complaints showed that 42% of  such complaints were outside 
the purview of the scheme, 23% were first resort co mplaints and 24% could not be 
considered for reasons like they were from unrelate d complainants or they required 
elaborate documentary and oral evidence or they wer e pending in other fora etc.  
Thus, effectively out of the total cases rejected, redressal could not be done only in 
11% cases as deficiency of service could not be established in these cases. 
 
(C) Web based mechanism may be set up for prompt/tr ansparent redressal of 
complaints under the scheme. 
 
A Complaint Tracking Software has already been oper ational for facilitating the 
complaint redressal function of the Banking Ombudsm an Offices. The software 
facilitates easy access to complete information abo ut the complaints, correspondence 
with the banks 
. 
 
(D) Awards involving small amounts say up to Rs.500 0/- may be kept out of the 
purview of the appeal to the Appellate Authority for speedier redressal. 
 
The suggestion is acceptable, though the experience is that no such appeals have been 
received from the banks.  However, the complainants  may continue to be allowed 
to appeal regardless of the amount 
. 

 
( E) The number of officers of the Ombudsman may be  suitably increased from the 
existing strength of 15 to improve the geographical  reach for the customers.  
Setting up of sub offices at smaller/remote centers can also be examined. 
 
The existing number of Banking Ombudsman offices at  15 does not appear to be a 
constraint in terms of geographical reach, particul arly as the availability of Banking 
Ombudsman Scheme is well advertised by both Banking Ombudsman (BO) as well as 
banks.  A BO could be approached even through an in expensive mode like post card.  
Moreover, BO conducts awareness campaigns in distri ct and other places in his area 
and even at times holds open meetings with bank cus tomers and others at such places 
to generate awareness of the scheme.  Sometimes eve n conciliation meetings are held 
at such places so that the complainant is not put t o any inconvenience.  Further, 
conciliation meetings are not compulsory and compla ints can be resolved by 
mediation through other modes like correspondence w ith the bank and the 
complainant 
 
The Committee does not agree with the RBI on the is sue of adequacy of the BOs 
and it feels that only 15 BOs all over the country are not adequate to handle 
huge amount of pending cases. The Committee recomme nds that RBI should 
appoint adequate number of BOs at the earliest.   
 
(F) The Scheme should be publicized by the banks in  both English and 
vernacular/local languages. 
 
The Banking Ombudsman Scheme booklet is published b y RBI in English and Hindi.  
In some states, it is publicized in local languages.  The suggestion is noted and will be 
implemented in all regions. The Ministry of Finance  concurs with the comments of 
the RBI. 
 

The Committee appreciates that the RBI is in agreem ent with some of the above 
suggestions. And accordingly recommends that the RB I should implement such 
suggestions expeditiously. 
 
11.  In June 2009, the Committee decided to revisit the issue in context of RRBs and 
Cooperative banks operating in remote hilly region of Himanchal Pradesh. 
Accordingly the Committee heard the presentations m ade by the Parvatiya bank, HP 
State Cooperative Bank and Kangra Central Cooperati ve Bank during its study visit 
to Himanchal Pradesh on 13 th  June 2009 (Annexure IX).  Subsequently the 
Committee also interacted with the representatives of Himanchal Grameen Bank on 
16 th  June 2009 at Manali (Annexure X).  
 
12.  The Committee noted with reservation that majority of the complaints were 
against the private banks followed by SBI group. It  also observed that the number of 
e-mail and online complaints are on the rise. 40% o f the complaints received by 
Ombudsman are first resort complaints meaning that the customer directly approach 
Ombudsman without first going to the bank for redre ssal of his grievance (s). The 
Committee was informed that most of the cases went in favour of the banks. 
 
13.  The Committee was  apprehensive that the pattern of  case being decided in 
favour of Banks  could be because of the resources and institutional support 
which the Banks  had to present their cases before the Ombudsman, while 
individual customers, especially the poor, did not have adequate means to 
present their cases and were at a disadvantage. 
 
14.  The Committee was informed that complaints were ver y few against the cooperative 
banks. 
 
15.  The Committee was of the view that lower numbers of  complaints against 
cooperative banks could be because the customers we re not aware of the 
scheme. The Committee reiterated the need for incre asing awareness of the 

scheme among the bank customers. The Committee felt  that there is a need 
to senisitize the bank staff towards the needs of the customers. 
 
Observations and recommendations of the Committee  
 
16.  The Committee considers that there is proliferation  of NBFCs and Private 
Financing Companies often approved by the RBI. As s uch, the Committee 
recommends that definition of Banks as given in Cla use 3(5) of Chapter I 
should be amended to include NBFCs, Private Financi ng Companies 
approved by the RBI and the Private Companies accepting the term deposits. 
 
17.  Regarding Clause 4(1) of Chapter II, the Committee considers that in 
addition to the CGM and GM of the RBI, retired Bank  officers not below the 
rank of General Manager who are conversant with customer relations should 
also be considered for Banking Ombudsman. In this r espect the Committee 
disagrees with RBI’s reply that appointment the sen ior Bank officer as 
Banking Ombudsman may result in conflict of interests.  
 
18.  Regarding Clause 7(1) of Chapter III on the jurisdi ction, the Committee 
considers that often the case may involve more than  one Bank located in 
different territorial jurisdiction. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the above Clause read with Clause 15 (3) must be accordingly elaborated. 
 
19.  Regarding Clause 7(5), the Committee recommends tha t the annual Report 
submitted by the Banking Ombudsman to RBI should ou tline the 
shortcomings and contain recommendations for struct ural modifications in 
Banking.  
 
20.  The Committee considers that the grounds for redres sal of grievances as 
detailed in Clause 8 of Chapter IV pertain largely to retail Banking services. 
The Committee feels that Credit card has rapidly em erged as a distinct 
business. Keeping in view the large number of compl aints and litigations 

pertaining to credit card business, the Committee f eels that regulation is 
necessary for the healthy growth of this Sector. It  is necessary that there 
should be transparency about the interest rates, du es and compounding of 
such dues. The obligations of the Banks providing t he credit card services 
should be clearly defined.  The Committee recognize s the steps taken by the 
Banks in educating the customers at different stage s, however, the terms and 
conditions are not adequately and distinctly inform ed to the customers at the 
time he seeks a credit card from the Bank. Often th e credit card marketing 
business is outsourced to marketing agencies, who o ften do not adhere to 
standard fair practices. It is, therefore, realisti cally assumed that the 
unsuspecting customers need education even before a  credit card is issued. 
The Committee also notes that the credit card busin ess is mostly outsourced 
by the Banks, thereby resulting in complete loss of  interface between the 
banks and the customer. Such an arrangement also ma kes it difficult to fix 
the responsibilities.  Also, while subscribing a cr edit card has been made 
much convenient by marketing agencies, discontinuation/cancellation of card 
is much more complex and difficult. Therefore, the Banking Ombudsman 
should clearly prescribe rules for outsourcing the services in respect of credit 
card business and the eventual obligations towards the redressal of 
complaints. The Committee acknowledges that the RBI  has issued guidelines 
in respect of credit card business.  Such guideline s should be incorporated as 
a separate Clause in the Chapter IV as the ground f or redressal of 
grievances. The Committee also feels that in view o f growing complaints 
against the credit card dues, the Committee conside rs that respective banks 
should have a separate grievance redressal cell and  that the RBI should 
consider appointing dedicated Ombudsman in existing  locations to deal with 
Credit card issues in line with RBI guidelines.  
 
21.  Clause 8 (2) of Chapter IV also provides deficienci es in servicing loans and 
advances as the ground for redressal. The Committee  has noted that such a 
clause is an acknowledgement by the RBI that despit e Government’s 
guarantees and refinancing facilities, there are st ill complaints about Banks 

being unwilling to give loans under the Government- schemes. The 
Committee recommends that the Banking Ombudsman sho uld specially 
monitor the bank lendings to marginalised sections and farmers under 
Government schemes. The Committee reiterates that t hese Schemes must be 
publicized by the Banks. The Committee recommends t hat RBI should make 
survey of the expenditures made by the Banks on pro moting/publicizing the 
personal loans vis a vis   on Government schemes meant for marginalized 
sections. Such a survey should illustrate, if the b anks are more inclined to 
promote commercial personal loans instead of Govern ment schemes. The 
Committee strongly feels that Banking Ombudsman sho uld conduct a survey 
of the procedural resistance faced by the potential  beneficiaries in availing 
the schemes and make commensurate recommendations. The Committee 
feels that advances and loans given under Governmen t’s social sector 
schemes should a dealt by the Banking Ombudsman as a separate class of 
cases and should be accorded special provisions. Th erefore, the Clause 8 
should accordingly be amended.  
 
22.  Clause 8 ( 2) refers to non-observance of RBI direc tive on interest rates as 
one of the ground for redressal. The Committee find s that in most of the 
cases the interest rates are benchmarked with PLR. However, the calculation 
of PLR remains opaque and the Bank PLR rates are no t adequately 
publicized. This is particularly vital for the Gove rnment schemes that 
provide for Bank loans at concessional or susidised  rates below the PLR. As 
such, the potential beneficiaries are denied the be nefit of the Scheme. The 
Committee, therefore,  recommends that RBI and Ombu dsman should 
ensure that the Banks while publicizing the Governm ent schemes should 
specifically mention the interest rate applicable t o the scheme. The 
Ombudsman should ensure the clarity and transparenc y in interest rates 
applicable to Government schemes.  
 
23.  The Clause 9 (1) prevents a customer from represent ing his case through a 
lawyer. The Committee failed to appreciate the rati onale behind such 

disabling provision and wondered if there was a mec hanism to identify such 
distinction. The Clause though does not impose any restriction on the Bank. 
The Committee finds that on the one hand, the custo mer is required to 
represent his own case or through a representative on the other hand the 
Banks’ case will be represented by their legal cell .  The Committee is of the 
opinion that an individual customer on its own woul d always find it difficult 
to match with the resources and institutional suppo rt which the Banks have. 
These apprehensions have been duly illustrated in t he admission that most of 
the cases filed with Banking Ombudsman went in favo ur of Banks. The 
Committee also recognized the fact that a large num ber of cases were 
rejected by the Banking Ombudsman as they were firs t resort complaints 
without exploring the redressal through the grievan ce redressal of 
mechanism of the concerned Bank. The Committee cons iders that instead of 
rejecting, such cases should be taken as an illustr ation of lack of faith in the 
grievance redressal mechanism of the Banks and such  cases must be referred 
by the Ombudsman to the concerned Bank for redressa l instead of rejecting 
them outright.  The Ombudsman which rely on the rec ords, should also 
survey the grievance redressal mechanism of the Ban ks and the grounds of 
rejections at that level. The Banking Ombudsman sho uld report to the RBI 
the functioning of grievance redressal mechanisms adopted by the Banks and 
increasing number of cases resorting to appeal to t he Ombudsman against 
the Banks. The Committee, therefore, recommends tha t the Clause 9(1) 
should be accordingly amended to allow an advocate to represent the case.  
 
24.  In This respect the Committee considers it relevant  to mention that only a 
few cases against cooperative banks and RRBs have r eached the Banking 
Ombudsman. The Committee apprehends that this could  be due to lack of 
awareness or apathy among the customers towards gri evance redressal 
mechanism. The Committee, therefore, recommends tha t the Banking 
Ombudsman Scheme should be widely publicized in rur al and semi-rural 
areas. It is incumbent upon the Banking Ombudsman a s the forum of first 
appeal to ensure that the RRBs and the Cooperative banks should widely 

publicise their grievance redressal mechanism in lo cal languages. The 
Committee also requires that the Ombudsman should r eflect in their report 
to the RBI, on the issue of grievance redressal mec hanism in RRBs and 
Cooperative banks. The Committee also recommends th at the grievance 
redressal mechanism in RRBs should be decentralized  and should be 
independent of the sponsor-nationalised Bank.  
 
25.  Regarding Clause 9 (3) (c) the Committee recommends  that the rulings given 
by the Banking Ombudsman should be compiled and pub lished by the RBI 
for larger dissemination.  
 
26.  In conclusion, the Committee feels that the Banking  Ombudsman scheme 
holds immense promise for the redressal of customer  grievances. With the 
emergence of newer banking products and with Banks becoming the primary 
lending institutions alongwith other credit institu tions like NBFCs, the 
grievances too are likely to multiply. Therefore, t he mandate of the Banking 
Ombudsman too should expand accordingly. The Commit tee, therefore, 
recommends that number and locations of Banking Omb udsman should be 
increased and new banking services and credit institutions should be brought 
under their purview. The Committee recommends that the Banking 
Ombudsman should incorporate elaborate recommendati ons in their annual 
Reports to the RBI and the RBI should regularly rev iew the its Guidelines in 
light of such recommendations.  
 
27.  Appreciating that the RBI has agreed to several sug gestions, the Committee 
expects that those suggestions shall be implemented  expeditiously and also 
recommends that the current Banking Ombudsman Schem e 2006 should be 
reviewed with reference to its recommendations.

INTRODUCTION 
1. I, the Chairman of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, 
having been authorized by the Comm ittee to present the Report on its 
behalf, do hereby present this One Hu ndred and Eighty Fourth Report of 
the Committee. 
1.2 The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting 
held on the 14th July, 2009 
1.3  The matter examined by the Committee arise out of the scrutiny of 
various Rules/Regulations and issues, relating to them along with the 
comments received from the Government. The observations and 
recommendations of the Committee ar e contained in the succeeding 
paragraphs of the Report. 
 
 
DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA  A. HEPTULLA
