ANNEXURE-X 
WRITTEN  REPLIES  TO  THE  POINTS  RAISED  DURING  
ORAL EVIDENCE  BEFORE  THE  COMMITTEE  ON  
SUBORDINATE LEGISLATION,  RAJYA  SABHA,  HELD  ON  
26.8.2008,  ON  BIO-MEDICAL  WASTE  (MANAGEMENT  &  
HANDLING)  RULES,  1998 
1.  Issue: The constraints encountered in implementing the BMW 
Rules. 
  Reply: (i) Segregation of infected BMW from the general and 
innocuous waste is the key factor for effective management of 
BMW. Many Government/private hospitals do not provide 
adequate funds for providing necessary equipments such as bins 
and colour coded plastic bags for segregation of infected BMW at 
source. 
  (ii) The paramedical staff such as nurses, wardboys and 
karamcharis, are not aware of proper segregation and handling of 
BMW and also the BMW Rules due to lack of proper awareness 
and training programmes. 
  (iii) Several hospitals send the mixed BMW of infectious as well as 
non-infectious nature to the municipal dump sites, contaminating 
the entire municipal waste.  
  (iv) In several States, there are no adequate common treatment 
facilities/incinerators for proper treatment and disposal of BMW 
generated in small health care facilities. 
  (v) Many small health clinics/nursing homes in the name of 
servicing less than 1000 patients per month, do not apply for 
authorization to the respective SPCBs/PCCs and go scot-free from 

the monitoring net of  the SPCBs/PCCs. Thereby sending the BMW 
to municipal dumpsites. 
  (vi) Due to inadequate manp ower, the SPCBs/PCCs  are not in a 
position to effectively monitor and take necessary action against the 
HCEs non-complying with the BMW Rules. 
  (vii) Many hospitals having their own captive incinerators are 
inefficient in controlling the emissions and meeting the stipulated 
standards because either they have single chamber incinerators, or 
incinerators without air pollution control systems. 
  (viii) Many hospitals also do not provide for proper treatment of 
their liquid effluents. 
  (ix) Several hospitals do not have the necessary facilities such as 
autoclaves, microwaves and shredd ers for proper disinfection and 
mutilation of the infected BMW. 
  (x) The doctors and superintendents of hospitals do not take 
management of BMW seriously and, therefore, do not provide the 
necessary equipments and manpower for proper management of 
BMW. 
  (xi) Considering the fact that ho spitals provide health services to 
the people, the SPCBs/PCCs usually do not consider to take 
necessary legal action such as di sconnection of electricity/water 
and closing down the hospitals. Therefore, the hospitals also do not 
take proper management of BMW seriously. 
2.  Issue: Are there any overlappings with regard to the jurisdictions of 
functions/responsibilities of MoEF, Ministry of Health and Family 
:Welfare (MoH&FW) and Ministry of Urban Development 
(MoUD) in  implementing the Rules. 

  Reply: The main function of MoEF as an Administrative Ministry 
of BMW Rules, is to ensure that the Rules are properly 
implemented by the respective SPCBs/PCCs and CPCB for proper 
management of infected BMW. The MoEF also undertakes 
promotional activities such as providing financial support for 
conducting awareness and training programmes to the medical and 
para-medical staff for effective management of BMW and 
implementing of the BMW Rules. It also makes necessary 
amendments to the Rules and develop necessary guidelines for 
proper management of BMW through the CPCB. 
  The MoH&FW being the administrative Ministry for promotion of 
health of the people, is responsible to ensure provision of adequate 
equipments for segregation of infected BMW, treatment and 
disposal facilities for the waste in the hospitals under their 
jurisdiction. They are also respon sible for conducting training and 
awareness programmes to the hospital staff. They also develop 
guidelines for effective management of BMW. 
  The MoUD being the administrative Ministry for proper 
management of municipal solid waste (MSW), is responsible to 
ensure that the infectious BMW generated at HCEs is not carried 
away along with the n on-infectious MSW. In case any hospital is 
not segregating the infectious BM W from the general waste, they 
can refuse to take such  waste from such hospitals and they are also 
required to inform the concerned SPCB/PCC for taking necessary 
action against the hospital. 
  From the above mentioned functions of various authorities it 
appears that each authority is having their own respective functions 

and responsibilities. However, certain functions are also 
overlapping. 
3.  Issue: Why it took 12 years to notify BMW Rules after the 
enactment of E(P) Act, 1986. 
  Reply: The necessity for notifying the Rules pertaining to bio-
medical waste management was felt after the directions were issued 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court for installation of pollution control 
devices in hospitals of Delhi, in the matter of B.L. Wadhera Versus 
Union of India in the year 1995. Later, the Ministry of Environment 
and Forests issued a draft notification inviting objections from the 
public in October, 1997 and thereafter the Bio-medical Waste 
(Management & Handling) Rules, 1998, were notified in July, 
1998. 
  The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 does not specify any time 
limit for notifying any Rules under it. The same are notified for 
various subjects as when the need for notifying the Rules on any 
subject is felt, as has happened in the case of Hazardous Waste 
(Management & Handling) Rules, 1989, Municipal Waste 
(Management & Handling) Rules, 2000, The Batteries 
(Management & Handling) Rules, 2001 etc. After the enactment of 
the E(P) Act, such Rules have been notified before as well as after 
the notification of BMW Rules under the E(P) Act. Still several 
Rules are being notified as per the need and requirement for 
protection of’ environment. Therefore, notification of various Rules 
under the E(P) Act is a continuous process and the same are 
notified as and when the same required. 
4.  Issue: What are the methods adopted in advanced countries for 
management of BMW. 

  Reply: The bio-medical wastes are commonly treated by 
incineration/autoclaving/microwaving/chemical disinfection in 
advanced countries. Common and ce ntralized facilities are also 
being practised in these countries as being practiced in our country. 
Following are the methods, being followed in some of the advanced 
countries: 
Technologies/Methods being adopted in advanced countries 
USA: 
  More than 90 per cent of potentially infectious medical waste is 
incinerated. In August 1997, EPA promulgated regulations governing the 
emissions from medical waste incinerators (MWIs). These regulations 
include: 
z  Stringent air emission guidelines for States to use in 
developing plans to reduce air pollution from medical waste 
incinerators built on or before June 20, 1996. 
z Final air emission standards fo r medical waste incinerators 
built after June 20, 1996. 
  These guidelines and standards will substantially reduce the 
emissions from the MWI. 
  One anticipated outcome by adoption of the new MWI standards 
and guidelines is the exploration of use of alternative technologies for 
treating medical waste. Due to the high cost of compliance with the MWI 
standards, EPA expects that few health care facilities are likely to install 
new MWIs and that many facilities are likely to discontinue use of 
existing MWIs. “EPA expects that operation of 50 to 80 per cent of the 
2,400 existing MWIs could be discontinued. As an alternative to MWIs, 

treatment facilities are likely to switch over to other methods of waste 
disposal such as off-site centralize d disposal facilities or onsite 
disinfection technologies. Some potential alternative treatment 
technologies include thermal treatment ( e.g., microwave technologies), 
steam sterilization ( e.g., autoclaving), electropyrolysis, and other 
chemical and mechanical systems. 
  Many States in USA have regulations requiring medical waste 
treatment technologies to be certified, licensed, or regulated. Individual 
States have their own requirements. 
Germany: 
  The specific treatment of clinical waste (waste from health service 
facilities) concentrates on a relati vely small portion of the total waste 
generated by these facilities. A maximum of 5 % (roughly 5,000 tonne 
per annum) of the total waste generated by hospitals and other health 
service facilities consists of infectious waste, along with organs and body 
parts. This waste must be treated us ing a thermal process specified by the 
Robert Koch Institute. Methods allowed include sterilisation/disinfection 
using steam, or incineration. Germany operates one stand-alone 
incinerator for special clinical waste in Kiel/Wellsee. In two municipal 
waste incineration plants (Augsburg and Bielefeld) infectious waste is 
incinerated in separate incineration units. To reduce emissions, the flue 
gas formed is channelled into the municipal waste incinerator’s flue gas 
treatment plant. As is normally the case with all centralised treatment 
solutions, a part of the infectious wa ste is transported to hazardous waste 
incinerators in containers licensed for the purpose. 
 
 

UK: 
  At the present time a number of  hot-oil, autoclave/microwave, 
chemical disinfection and steam sterilisation systems are known to be 
licensed and operating at a merchant commercial scale in the UK. These 
facilities do not handle recognisab le anatomical waste for aesthetic 
reasons as all identifiable human tissu es, whether infected or not, are 
supposed to be disposed of by incineration. One gasification plant is also 
known to be licensed and operating at a merchant commercial scale in the 
UK. 
5.  Issue: Is there any scheme/system for BMW collection from 
various health care facilities in the country. 
  Reply: As per the provisions of BMW Rules, it is the responsibility 
of the generation of BMW to segregate, collect, store, transport, treat and 
dispose of the BMW, as per the tr eatment methods prescribed in the 
Rules either in his own premises or in a common treatment facility. 
  There are 149 Common Bio-medical Waste Treatment Facilities 
(CBWTFs) and other 8 are yet to commission/trial basis/under installation 
in the country as on March, 2007. These CBWTFs collect bio-medical 
wastes from various healthcare facil ities and transport for treatment and 
disposal. State-wise details are given in the Annexure. 
6.  Issue: How segregation of hazardous BMW and non-hazardous 
BMW is done. 
  Reply: As per the BMW Rules, the segregation of infectious BMW 
has to be done and the segregated waste has to be put in different colour--
coded bins for appropriate treatment and disposal non-hazardous waste is 
segregated separately and sent to municipal landfills. 

  The sub-rule (1) of Rule (6) of Bio-medical Waste (Management & 
Handling) Rules, 1998 states that bio-medical waste shall not be mixed 
with other wastes. Further, sub-rule (2) of the Rule  (6) stipulates that bio-
medical waste shall be segregated into-containers/bags at the point of 
generation in accordance with Schedule II prior to its storage, 
transportation, treatment and disposal. The containers shall be labelled 
according to Schedule III of the BMW Rules. 
  The Schedule II of the Rules specifies colour coding and type of 
containers for disposal of bio-medical wastes. The stipulated colour 
codings are yellow, red, blue/white translucent and black for different 
categories of wastes. 
7.  Issue: Whether incineration of BMW is causing pollution. 
  Reply: The incineration of bio-medical wastes is one of the 
stipulated treatment methods in the Bio-medical Waste (Management & 
Handling) Rules, 1998. The Rules further stipulate operating and 
emission standards of incinerator in order to check adverse affect to 
human health and environment. The standards stipulate provisions of 
combustion efficiency, temperatures in the chambers, stack height and 
limit of various pollutants such as particulate matters, Nitrogen Oxides, 
Hydrochloric Acid (HCI) and volatile organic compounds. Further, in 
order to avoid formation of toxic pollutants, the Rules have prohibited the 
incineration of chlorinated plastic waste and wastes treated with any 
chlorinated disinfectants. If the incinerator meets these standards, 
pollution due to incineration will be minimal without causing any adverse 
effect on environment. 
8.  Issue: How the needles/syringes are dealt with after use. 

  Reply: The needles have been categorized under ‘waste sharps’ in 
the Schedule-I of the BMW Rules. After use, the needles are required to 
be broken and destructed in a needle cutter kept in the hospitals at each 
location wherever the injections are given. The waste sharps shall be 
disinfected by chemical treatment/autoclaving/microwaving followed by 
mutilation/shredding. The rules do not have provisions for disposal of 
wastes after imparting requisite treatment as stipulated in the Rules. 
However, the guidelines on common bio-medical waste treatment facility 
prepared by CPCB recommends for dis posal of disinfected sharps in 
secured municipal landfills. 
  Issue: Whether there is any check on the private common treatment 
facilities. 
  Reply: The private Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment Facility 
(CBMWTF) operators are required to obtain authorization from the 
respective SPCB/PCC of UT before setting of such facility as per Rule-9 
of the BMW Rules. The SPCBs/PCCs issue such authorization with 
certain conditions for proper treatment and disposal of BMW. 
Subsequently, the SPCBs/PCCs of UTs inspect and monitor these 
facilities to verify compliance to the conditions stipulated. The CPCB 
also randomly checks such facilities and wherever the facilities are found 
not complying with the stipulated conditions, necessary action is taken by 
the respective SPCB/PCC of UT, including closure of such facility. 
10.  Issue: Whether the private hospi tals are also following the norms 
like the Government hospitals. 
  Reply: As per the BMW Rules, all the healthcare facilities are 
required to comply with the prescribed norms/standards irrespective of 
whether they are private or Govern ment hospitals. Necessary action can 
be taken by the respective SPCB/PCC for non-compliance. As per the 

Rule (4) of the BMW Rule it shall be the duty of every occupier of an 
institution generating bio-medical waste which includes a hospital, 
nursing home, clinic, dispensary, veterinary, animal house, pathological 
laboratory, blood bank by whatever name called to take all steps to ensure 
that such waste is handled without any adverse effect to human health and 
the environment. The BMW Rules, therefore, are applicable to all bio-
medical waste generators irrespective of whether Government or Private 
owned. 
11.  Issue: Is there any provision for issuing certificates like ISO, for 
hospitals. 
  Reply: There is no provision in the BMW Rules for issuing such 
certificates like ISO to hospitals. 
12.  Issue: The BMW incineration ash contains some hazardous 
chemicals contaminating water and soil, if not properly disposed of. How 
this is dealt with? 
  Reply: As per the Schedule II of the BMW Rules, the incineration 
ash is required to be segregated in black colour plastic bags and disposed 
of in a secured landfill. The same is not allowed for disposal on land or in 
water bodies. By disposing on secure landfills, leaching of hazardous 
chemicals, if any, is prevented. 
13.  Issue: What are the problems the hospitals are facing? Which are 
the agencies that are involved into it and where does the real problem lie? 
We would also like to know the Ministry’s views and suggestions for 
making the implementation of the existing rules more effective, or, if any 
amendments are needed thereto. 
  Reply: The real problem faced by hospitals in complying with the 
BMW Rules is proper segregation of the infected BMW. Since only about 

15% is the infected BMW and 85% is uninfected and innocuous general 
municipal waste, by proper segregation the quantity of waste required to 
be treated and disposed of will be minimized. Another problem for proper 
management of BMW is lack of awareness and training of the 
stakeholders for proper handling and segregation of BMW. Other 
problems include, lack of adequate trained manpower, non-availability of 
funds for procuring the required materials and equipments as well as for 
treatment and disposal of BMW by the hospitals. The agencies 
responsible for implementation of the BMW Rules, namely, SPCBs/PCCs 
of UTs are also short of manpower to inspect and monitor the issued 
authorizations and take follow-up actions against the violators of the 
Rules. The State Pollution Control Board (SPCB)/Pollution Control 
Committee (PCC) is the prescribed authority for implementation of 
provisions of the Rules in the respective State/UT. Recently, Central 
Pollution Control Board conducted an interaction meet on 08/8/2008 at 
New Delhi where representatives from various SPCBs/PCCs, Deptt. of 
Health of some States/UTs, CBWTF facility operators, IMA and some 
bigger hospitals participated. An action plan including policy for 
implementation of the BMW Rules and amendments required in the 
BMW Rules were discussed and th e same has been sent to all 
SPCBs/PCCs for their comments so as to initiate necessary action for its 
implementation. Further, implementation of the Bio-Medical Waste 
(Management & Handling) Rules, 1998 and amendments thereof involve 
watch on healthcare facilities which are operating in quite a large 
numbers in every State/UT. The manpower mainly available in 
SPCBs/PCCs and CPCB are already stretched with priority and 
voluminous areas of implementation such as Water Act, Air Act, 
Environment (Protection) Act, Hazardous Waste(Management & 
Handling) Rules, Court matters etc. Inadequate availability of manpower 
and requisite infrastructure in SPCBs/PCCs and CPCB is also a problem 

for effective incomplete implementation of the Bio-medical Waste 
(Management & Handling) Rules, 1998 and amendments thereof. 
14.  Issue: The Committee would like to  know the facilities available in 
our hospitals. We would like to know, according to the Act, which was 
passed in Parliament, what measures have been taken for the disposal of 
bio-medical waste? How do you dispose it of and what pattern are you 
following? In case, some people are violating those rules and hospitals 
are not complying with it, what action the Ministry of Health as well as 
the Ministry of Environment is taking? What punishments are there and 
what regulations are applied for it? We would like to have brief 
information. 
  Reply: As per the BMW Rules, provisions are made for treatment 
and disposal of various categories of BMW by adopting different 
treatment methods. The treatment methods include incineration deep 
burial, autoclave/microwave disinf ection, chemical disinfection; 
shredding and disposal into secured landfills. Some large hospitals in the 
country have their own treatment and disposal facilities such as 
incinerator, autoclave/hydroclave/microwave and shredder for treating 
bio-medical wastes, while small hospitals/clinics get the same treated and 
disposed of at the common treatment facilities available in their 
respective State/UT. The BMW Ru les were notified under the 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (EP Act). The EP Act provides 
penalties for non-compliance of the Rules made under the Act. As per 
Section-5 of the EP Act, directions can be issued by the concerned 
SPCB/PCC to the violating units for its closure. Directions can also be 
issued to the concerned authorities to disconnect electricity/water or any 
other service for non-complying units under Section-5 of the E(P) Act. 

  Further, the section 15 of the Act stipulates provisions of penalty 
for contravention of the provisions of the act and the Rules, orders and 
directions and the same is reproduced as below: 
(1) Whoever fails to comply with or contravenes any of the 
provisions of this Act, or the rules made or orders or 
directions issued thereunder, shall, in respect of each such 
failure or contravention, be punishable with imprisonment for 
a term which may extend to five years with fine which may 
extend to one lakh rupees, or  with both, and in case the 
failure or contravention continues, with additional fine which 
may extend to five thousand rupees for every day during 
which such failure or contravention continues after the 
conviction for the first such failure or contravention. 
(2) If the failure or contravention referred to ill sub-section (1) 
continues beyond a period of one year after the date of 
conviction, the offender shall be punishable with 
imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years. 
15.  Issue: Very often we mention guidelines. Now rules have come out. 
Is there any provision which clash w ith it or is that guidelines are 
supplementary to the rules. We are not very clear about that. Whether 
there is any executive instruction on that? 
  Reply: The BMW Rules are notified under the EP Act and the 
Rules will always be supreme vis-a-vis any guidelines which are issued. 
There is no clash between Rules and guidelines. Guidelines will help in 
implementation of the Rules. 

16.  Issue: Is there any mechan ism in place for monitoring and 
implementation at State as well as National level? This needs to be 
properly, adequately and comprehensively clarified by the Ministry? 
  Reply: As per the provisions of the BMW Rules, the respective 
SPCB/PCC is the prescribed authority for implementation and monitoring 
at the State/UT level. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) also 
randomly monitors the implementation of the BMW Rules in various 
States of the country. In case th e CPCB observes any violations of the 
Rules, it can direct the concerned SPCB/PCC to take necessary action 
against the defaulting units including closure of the unit. 
17.  Issue: Is there any provision for the closure of the hospitals 
violating the rules? 
  Reply: As per Section-5 of the EP Act, the respective SPCB/PCC 
of UT can issue closure orders of the hospitals for violating the Rules. 
18.  Issue: There was a ruling by the Supreme Court saying harsh 
actions needed to be taken against defaulters whether those concerns of 
the judiciary have been incorporated in the rules or not? 
  Reply: The Hon’ble Supreme Court has issued certain directions for 
taking necessary measures for non- compliance of the Rules against the 
defaulting hospitals which were duly considered while finalizing the 
BMW Rules. 
19.  Issue: There are 21 Central level common facilities for treatment of 
hazardous wastes (TSDFs). Are they adequate for the whole of India? 
  Reply: Presently, there are 21 common treatment, storage and 
disposal facilities (TSDFs) for proper disposal of hazardous wastes and 
some more are in the process of being developed in various States of the 

country. The States which are developi ng TSDFs are required to have an 
MoU signed with the neighbouri ng States which are having such 
facilities, for disposal of BMW till their own facilities are developed. 
20.   Issue: If the unit uses the common facilities for waste disposal do 
they charge something for that? 
  Reply: The units which use common TSDFs are required to become 
members of such facilities and pay for treatment and disposal of their 
wastes. 
21.  Issue: We wanted to be clearly spelt out the responsibilities? What 
are the proper division of functions between various Ministries, 
authorities and agencies like Boards so that it will be possible for us to 
make recommendations?  
  Reply: The role of the Ministry of Environment and Forests is to 
frame necessary rules and regulati ons for proper management of the 
BMW, which are uniformly applicable throughout the country. The 
Ministry also plays promotional role by providing necessary financial 
assistance for conducting training and awareness programmes regarding 
the BMW Rules. The Ministry of Urban Development is responsible for 
proper management of urban/munici pal waste which is non-infectious, 
generated from the hospitals. The SPCBs/PCCs of UTs are responsible 
for implementation of the BMW Rules. The Ministry of health is 
responsible for providing necessary infrastructure facilities in the 
hospitals for proper management of BMW. They are also responsible for 
developing necessary guidelines and supporting awareness and training 
programmes for hospital staff. Hence, the responsibilities of various 
authorities and Ministries are prov ided in the respective rules and 
regulations. 

22.  Issue: The status of Court cases in all State may be provided. 
  Reply: As per the information available with CPCB, the number of 
court cases against defaulting healthcare facilities as on March, 2007 is as 
below: 
Assam 01 
Bihar 06 
Chhattisgarh 12 
Himachal Pradesh 01 
Karnataka 01 
Maharashtra 01 
Madhya Pradesh 17

  The Committee wanted to know the method of disposal of bio-
medical waste in the hospitals and the problems and practical difficulties 
being faced by hospitals and the State Pollution Control Boards in the 
disposal of bio-medical waste. 
  The Committee was informed that the statutory body to oversee the 
implementation of the Bio-medical Waste Rules in Puducherry is the 
Puducherry Pollution Control Committee and in Tamil Nadu it is the 
Tamil Nadu Pollution Contral Board. It was also stated that as per the 
Guidelines, the generator of bio-medical waste is responsible for its 
segregation, management and disposal. The generators include doctors, 
nurses and other medical staff. 
  The Committee noted that colour-c oded polythene bags are used for 
identification and segregation of different types of wastes. For example, 
yellow bags for infected waste and black bags for general and non-
infected waste, etc. The various steps involved in waste management are 

generation, segregation, collection in specific colour bags, transportation, 
storage, treatment and final disposal. The various instruments used for 
bio-medical waste treatment are incinerator, autoclave, shredder, 
compactor, etc. 
  The Committee was informed that internal training programmes for 
hospital staff are conducted by the individual hospitals like JIPMER, 
Apollo and Christian Medical College, Vellore to spread awareness about 
the rules. The Committee was also informed that lack of awareness, lack 
of motivation, inadequate manpower and high cost of bio-medical waste 
disposal were some of the major constraints faced by the hospitals in the 
implementation of the rules. 
  The Committee notes that bio-medical waste management is given 
low priority and that there is still lack of awareness about the rules. A 
hospital may be very inefficient in the management of bio-medical wastes 
but it may still be rated as the best institute. 
  The Committee was also informed that private players are used for 
the collection and disposal of bio-medical waste. The Committee feels 
that the Government should take up this job instead of outsourcing it to 
private players. 
  The Committee recommends that special training in waste 
disposal/management should be impart ed to all employees in hospitals 
and that special courses could be started by the Ministry of Environment 
and Forests and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare regarding 
this. The Committee was informed that IGNOU had started a six month 
course on waste management but the Committee feels that IGNOU, being 
a distance education university, is not the right university to conduct the 
course. Bio-medical waste management, being a practical oriented field 

cannot be taught through correspondence courses. A uniform model for 
training should be prepared by the Ministry of Environment and Forests 
and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. 
  The Committee also wants the Ministry of Environment and Forests 
to explore the feasibility of providing grants/funds to NGOs to conduct 
awareness programs and seminars on the issue. 
  The Committee suggests that an enormous fee should be imposed 
for non-compliance with the rules so that the hospitals feel the pinch and 
act as a deterrent in future. The fee/fines may also be recovered from the 
salaries of officials found violating th e rules to ensure that the employees 
are more responsible and the rules strictly followed. The Committee feels 
that closing down an institution/hospital is not the solution as the patients 
are made to suffer for no fault of theirs. 
  The Committee also suggests that not only hospital but clinics and 
laboratories should also be brought under the purview of the Bio-medical 
Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 1998.

Rajya Sabha as the Parliament was adjourned Sine Die on 23.12.2008.” 
 The Committee regrets the delay in ‘laying of papers and recommends 
that Ministry should take the first available opportunity for laying the 
statutory Notifications and should not postpone this work for the later part of 
the session so that the eventualities like early prorogation of the House, which 

is of course rare, could be avoided. The Ministry of Home Affairs should take 
necessary corrective measures in right earn est so that they are able to cut on 
delays in laying of Notifications. 
(ix) Ministry of Huma n Resource Development 
 (Department of Higher Education)  
 The Ministry of Human Resource Development (Department of Higher 
Education) have laid 7 notifications and f our of these (Sl. No. 320, 322 to 324) 
have been delayed by five months to one and half year. There is no delay 
statement appended with them. 
 The Committee is unhappy to note that the Ministry of Human 
Resource Development (Department of  Higher Education) laid seven 
Notifications and four of them have been  delayed, The Notification at Sl. No. 
320 has a delay period of six months and Notification at Sl. No. 324 with a 
delay period of eight months. Two notifications at Sl. No. 322 and 323 have 
been delayed by one year six months a nd one year four months respectively. 
The Ministry have not appended any de lay statement with either of them. 
The Ministry of Human Resource De velopment (Department of Higher 
Education) have failed to lay the notifi cations fairly on time. If precaution 
had been taken, the Notifications co uld have been laid earlier. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should keep vigil for laying their 
Notifications at the earliest opportuni ty during the session so that extreme 
delays are avoided. Where there is delay,  Ministry should invariably apprise 
the House about the reason of delay through delay statement, in case they are 
unable to lay them in time. Th e Committee invites attention to 
recommendation contained in its 135th Report. 
(x)  Ministry of Rural Development 
 (Department of Rural Development)  

 Ministry of Rural Development (Department of Rural Development) have 
laid a total of 7 Notifications. Out of these two (Sl. No.379 and 380) have been 
delayed by seven months each and no delay statements are appended with them. 
 The Committee recommends that th e Ministry of Rural Development 
(Department of Rural Development) should take necessary corrective steps to 
ensure that such delays are not repeate d and that in case such delays do 
occur for unavoidable reasons, the same  should be conveyed to Parliament 
without fail by giving proper and adequate reasons in a delay statement. 
(xi) Ministry of Road Transport & Highways  
 The Ministry of Road Transport & Highways have laid 194 notifications on 
the Table of the House. 18 notifications have been delayed out of which 7 
notifications have been accompanied by delay statements and 11 delayed 
notifications have no delay statements appended with them. The delay period 
ranges from 5 months to six months. The delayed notifications which have been 
accompanied with delay statements have a delay period of 5 to 7 months. The 
reasons for delay given by the Ministry is as under:- 
 “It took some time to collect the papers and complete the procedural 
formalities. As such the notifications could not be laid on the Table of both the 
Houses of Parliament during the last session.” 
 The Committee notes with regret that  Ministry of Road Transport & 
Highways have appended delay statement only with seven of the eighteenth 
Notifications that were delayed. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry must have a re-look into th e cases of delay and try to plug the 
deficiencies so that such instances do not recur. They should also not fail to 
append delay statement in relevant cases in future. 
(xii) Ministry of Shipping  
 The Ministry of Shipping have laid nine Notifications out of which three 
Notifications (Sl. Nos. 585 to 587) have been delayed by five months. Delay 
statements are appended to with all of th em. The reasons cited by the Ministry for 
delay is given below: 

 “Due to delay in receiving the papers from Government Press and 
completing the formalities of authentication etc., the Notifications could not be 
sent on 20.2.2009 to Rajya Sabha Secretariat.” 
 The Committee observes that laying of Notifications in time on both the 
Houses of Parliament is a statutory obli gation on the part of the Ministry of 
Shipping. Being aware of that, the Mini stry should have taken immediate 
necessary steps to complete the formalit ies for laying of the papers. But the 
Ministry kept the matter pending t ill laying time approched. Had the 
Ministry been vigilant, the unnecessary delay would have been curbed. The 
Committee observes that the Ministry of  Shipping should review the cases of 
delay and devise remedial measures to av oid such instances of delay in laying 
of subordinate legislation. 
3. The Committee impresses upon all the Ministries/Departments to take 
immediate steps to ensure timely and proper laying of subordinate legislation. The 
Committee, accordingly, wishes to bring to the notice of all 
Ministries/Departments of the Government of India, particularly, the defaulting 
ones, the following recommendations, as contained in its 131st, 135th and 152nd 
Reports:- 
 “Orders required to be laid before th e House should be laid (i) if the 
House is not in Session, during the Sessi on immediately following the date of 
publication of the Order in the Official Gazette and (ii) if the House is in 
Session, on the date of the publication of the Order, during its continuance 
and in case the time lag between the da te of publication and the date of the 
closing of the Session is less than 15 clear days, before the expiry of the 
Session immediately followin g the said Session. All the 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India should henceforth comply 
with this schedule in the matter of layi ng of the Orders issued under various 
Acts of Parliament on the Table of the Rajya Sabha. 
(131st Report) 
(Presented on 15 December 2000) 
 “The Committee has, time and again , emphasized that it is essential 
that in case there is a de lay in the laying of Stat utory Orders, the concerned 
Ministry/Department should invariably append a delay statement along with 

the notifications being laid so as to apprise Parliament of the causes of delay. 
The Committee desires all Ministries/Departments to take a note of this, since 
the intention is that through the proces s of formulation of a delay statement 
the Ministry is able to introspect, id entify bottlenecks a nd devise remedial 
measures”. 
(135th Report) 
(Presented on 27 July 2001) 
 “In the opinion of the Committee, ever y notification should be assigned 
a distinctive number in order to give it a separate identity and similarly, no 
notification should be published/laid  which does not carry a notification 
number. The Committee expects all Mini stries/Departments of Government 
of India to exercise caution in this regard. In case where there are more than 
one notification under a single file, th e Ministries/Departments should ensure 
that the file number on each notificati on should be suitably distinguished 
from one another.” 
(152nd Report) 
(Presented on 26 August 2004)

INTRODUCTION 
 
 
1. I, the Chairman of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, having been 
authorized by the Committee, do hereby pr esent on its behalf, this One Hundred 
and Eighty Sixth Report of the Committee. 
 
 1.2     The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on 
the10th December, 2009 
 
1.3 The matters examined by the Committee arose in the process of scrutiny of 
the Municipal Solid Wastes (Managemen t and Handling) Rules, 2000 and issues 
relating to them along with the comments received from the Government.  The 
observations and recommendations of the Committee are contained in the 
succeeding paragraphs of the Report.  
 
.  
 
 
 
DR. (SHRIMATI) NAJMA A. HEPTULLA                            
                                                                                                               Chairperson 
 Committee on Subordinate Legislation, 
                                                                                                              Rajya Sabha 
 
NEW DELHI 
10th December, 2009 
 

 5
  
 
 
The Municipal Solid Wastes (Management & Handling) Rules, 2000 
 
Introduction  
The Central Government enacted the Municipal Solid Wastes (Management 
and Handling) Rules, 2000 ( Annexure I)  under Environment Protection Act, 
1986 ( Annexure II) to regulate the management and handling of the municipal 
solid wastes in environmentally acceptable manner. The rules have come into 
force from 25
th September 2000. Salient Features of the Rules are as follows: 
 
●  Municipal solid waste includes commercial and residential wastes generated 
in municipal or notified areas in either  solid or semi-solid from excluding 
industrial hazardous wastes but including treated bio-medical wastes 
● Rules are applicable to every munici pal authority responsible for collection, 
segregation, storage, transportation, pro cessing and disposal of municipal solid 
wastes. 
● Every municipal authority within the te rritorial area of the municipality is 
responsible for the implementation of th e provisions of these rules and for any 
infrastructure development for collection, storage, se gregation, transportation, 
processing and disposal of municipal solid wastes. 
● Local bodies were required to set up waste processing and disposal facilities 
before 31.12.2003. 
 
Guidelines/norms to be followed for handling municipal solid wastes have been 
provided in the Schedules and these relate to; 
 
• Prohibition of littering of solid wastes 
• Organizing house to house collection of waste 

 6
• Proper collection of waste from slums and squatters, hotels, restaurants, 
office complexes and commercial areas 
• Waste not be burnt 
• Organising awareness programmes for segregation of wastes  
•  Proper maintenance of waste storage facilities 
• Covering of vehicles used for transportation of wastes 
• Adopting suitable waste processing technol ogies to make use of wastes so 
as to minimize burden on landfill. 
•  Restricting land filling for non-biodegradable inert waste 
•  land filling operations to  follow prescribed proce dure to prevent pollution 
problem 
 
 
2     The Rules were examined and a questionnaire on the subject was 
forwarded to the Ministry of Envir onment & Forests for their comments/ 
clarifications on the 9 th July, 2001.  The Ministry furnished their comments/ 
clarifications on the 27th July, 2001 (Annexure III). The Committee considered 
the matter at its meeting held on the 16 th May, 2002 and made certain 
observations.  The Ministry fu rnished their comments on the 6 th November, 
2002 (Annexure IV).   
 
3     Upon the query that as “ the local Government, P ublic Health and 
sanitation at matters covered under the State list of the 7 th Schedule of the 
Constitution of India, the extent to which the Central Rules can suo-moto 
prescribe the responsibilities for the State Government, its officers and 
municipalities”, the Ministry of Environment and Forest ( MoEF) submitted in 
written reply  
 
“At the time of framing of Mu nicipal Solid Waste Management ( 
MSW) Rules, it was felt that although municipal waste 
management is governed by the bye-laws framed by respective 
municipal bodies, ev en better equipped municipal bodies like 

 7
Mumbai and Kolkata had hardly any regulations to set up 
scientifically designed land fill sites. As a result, serious ground 
water pollution was noticed in and around the Metros. It was 
therefore a conscious decision on the part of MoEF to notify 
through MSW Rules, uniform procedure for various aspects of 
handling of municipal waste , spec ification for land fill sites, 
standards for composting, leacha tes and incineration including 
standards for drinking water and am bient air quality with sole 
objective to prevent pollution of air, water and soil for which 
MoEF is fully competent to notify rules under EP Act, 1986.” 
 
 
4     The Committee also recogni sed that Municipal Solid Waste 
(Management and Handling) Rules, 2000 were notified in exercise of 
powers conferred under Sections 3, 6 and 25 of the Environment Protection 
Act, 1986. However it was observed by th e Committee that Section 3 of the 
said Act did not confer any Rule making powers to the Central Government. 
The Ministry in its written submission stated- 
“Under Section 3, Central Go vernment has the powers to 
take all such measures as is necessary or expedient for the 
purpose of protecting and improving the quality of 
environment and preventing, controlling and abating 
environmental pollution.” 
 
 
5      The Committee recognized that  the Section 3 of the Environment 
(Protection) Act, 1986, bestows sweep ing powers of setting standards, 
laying down procedures and supervis ion on the Central Government.  
However, the Committee underscored that  the Rules 4 (1) made municipal 
authority eventually responsible for the implementation of these Rules, 
under Rule 4(2) the State Pollution C ontrol Board has been entrusted with 
power of granting the authorization to  the municipal authority or other 
operator for setting up waste handling and processing facility. Rules 5 (1) 
and (2) puts overall responsibility of implementation of Rules on the Urban 
Development Department of the State Government and District 
Magistrate/Deputy Commissioner.  

 8
 
6      Upon being asked whether any m echanism was in place to ensure that 
the implementation of Rules and the Schedules there of were complied 
with, the Ministry of Environment and Forest replied- 
“The Municipal authorities are required to comply with 
the    implementation schedul e and seek authorization for 
setting up of waste processing and disposal facilities. The 
Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has been given 
the task of review of implementation and detection of non-
compliance. The State Pollution Control Boards (SPCB)/ 
Committees have been delegated powers under the Section 
5 of the Environment (Protect ion) Act to give direction. 
This empowers the SPCB/Committees to give directions to 
ensure compliance by th e municipal authorities 
concerned. In case of non- compliance Section 19 powers 
to take cognizance of offence is already delegated to the 
State Government.” 
 
7     Upon being enquired as to what was meant by the “overall responsibility” 
to the Department of Urban Developm ent of the State Government and the 
District Magistrate/Deputy Commissioner, the MoEF replied:  
 
“The word ‘overall responsibil ity’ means that the state 
authorities are required to en sure the implementation of 
provisions of the Rules. Since the subject of the legislation 
on municipal solid waste co llection, transportation and 
disposal is under the jurisdic tion of Department of Urban 
Development in the State and with the Deputy 
Commissioner at the District level, these authorities have 
been identified as officers responsible to oversee 
implementation.” 
 
8       Upon being enquired about the powers being conferred upon these 
officers under the Act and these Rules to  enable them to  discharge their 
responsibilities, it was further stated that “All these authorities have been 
delegated powers under Sections 5, 10, 11 and 19 of the Environment 

 9
(Protection) Act, 1986 which deals with powers to give directions, entry and 
inspection, sampling and taking cognizance of offence respectively.” 
 
9 Constraints in implementation of MSW Rules. 
 
• In a written submission to the Committee on 2 nd October 2002 ( Annexure 
V), the Ministry of Environment and Fo rest recognized th e constraints and 
difficulties faced in implementation of the Rules based on the feedback 
received from SPCBs and local bodies within two years of application: 
 
• Inadequate financial resources to undertake improvement in management of 
municipal solid waste as per Schedule-II, III and IV of the Rules; 
 
• Lack of technical assistance to loca l bodies for selection of appropriate 
waste processing and disposal technologies; and  
 
• Inadequate provision of training to all cadres of officials. 
 
10 Proposed Action Plan for the management of municipal solid waste:
 
 
      The Ministry of Environment and Forest informed the Committee that an 
Action Plan was prepared under which the urban clusters have been categorized 
according to population and waste-generation: 
 
Action Plan for cities generating waste- more than 500 tonnes/ day 
 
• For Cities generating municipal solid waste (MSW) more than 500 t/d, the 
action plan may include the following component; 
 
• Modernization/mechanization of waste storage and transportation facilities; 

 10
• Privatization/contract with 'opera tors' for collection of waste and 
transportation; 
• Private entrepreneurship in setting up of waste processing and disposal 
facility. 
 
Action Plan for cities generating waste between 100-500 tonnes per /day 
 
     There wee 70 cities (2002) in the country generating waste between 100-500 
t/d. The towns generating waste ra nging 100-500 tonnes per day, needed 
strengthening of collection, storage a nd transportation of waste. There was 
possibility that a single plant (up to 500 t/d) could serve the purpose of waste 
processing. 
 
Action Plan for towns generating waste less than 100 tonnes/day 
 
     There were 58 towns (2002) ha ving population more than 50000 and waste 
generation between 50 to 100 t/d. These to wns did not requir e high cost waste 
processing and disposal technologies. Such towns should organize proper waste 
collection, storage and transportation system considering local situation. 
Aerobic composting could be an appropriate option for these towns. 
 
Towns having waste generation less than 50 tonnes/day 
 
     Majority of towns fall under this category and these are around 4239 (2002). 
Out of these, 506 were in Class I and II category of cities and remaining 3733 
towns were having populat ion less than 50,000. These towns needed simpler 
technological options, which could be managed without high skill operations. 
Main emphasis in such towns should  be on proper collection of waste and 
motivating people on segregation of wast e. Collected waste could easily be 
composted and used locally. 

 11
 
 
11 Requirement/Pre-requisites for implementation of Action Plan 
 
     The Ministry also recognized th e pre-requisite for the implementation of 
Action Plan 
 
At State level:    
 
      State Pollution Control Boards a nd local bodies at th e State level would 
need necessary support for implemen tation of the Municipal Solid Waste 
(Management and Handling) Rules. St ate government, local body and the 
concerned SPCB may collectively take up the following course of action: 
 
• Setting up of State level Steering Committee to oversee the progress of 
implementation of the Rules (under the Chairmanship of Chief Secretary/or 
Secretary, Urban Development). 
• Setting up Monitoring Committee at District  level to review the progress of 
implementation of the rules of all the cities/towns at District level (under 
the Chairmanship of Development Commissioner/Collector) 
• Setting up State level Technology Adviso ry Group (STAG) to assist local 
bodies on selection of appropriat e waste processing and disposal 
technologies. 
• State Pollution Control Board may set up Advisory Group/Committee to 
assist the Board in; 
o Issuance of authorizations to local bodies 
o Identification of sites for future waste disposal si tes and sites for 
setting up of waste processing plan t in the State after taking public 
hearings into account. 
o Management of Accidents. 

 12
• SPCB will need to strengthen laboratory facilities to undertake monitoring 
of parameters stipulated for ensuring compliance to the standards. 
• State Government (concerned Department in the State) will need to 
formulate State Policy and Action Plan to prioritise the action required for 
compliance with the Rules. Such Polic y will address issues relating to; 
appropriate strengtheni ng of local bodies (techni cally and financially), 
waste processing and disposal facil ities including making provisions for 
future sites, and other relevant issues 
•  Preparation of State level directory containing information on institutions, 
experts, technology providers, consu ltants who could be approached for 
interaction on various issues. Howeve r, such directory will be only 
indicative and not bindi ng on the local body for finalizing the award of 
work, etc. 
• Identification of State level Instit utes for organizing training to the 
Municipal staff and other concerned of various cadres. 
• Enlisting NGOs, voluntary organizations in the State for seeking their 
participation including mass awarene ss and organizing proper collection, 
segregation and storage of waste. 
 
 
At Central level 
 
•  CPCB to set up Technology Apprai sal Committee (TAC) as required 
under Municipal Solid Waste Rules. 
• CPCB to undertake field studies relati ng to various aspects of management 
of MSW to back-up the Rules. Such st udies to cover technological aspects, 
environment impact assessment, epidemiological studies, review of 
standards, etc. 

 13
• CPCB to bring out codes, guidelines to assist State level organizations on 
issues like, review of technologies, identification of landfill sites, manual 
for analysis of parameters, etc. 
• Prepare an illustrative Directory on Technology providers, experts, 
institutions and consulta nts involved in manageme nt of municipal solid 
waste. Such Directory will be only for reference purpose and not for any 
award of work. 
•  Ministry of Environment and Forest s (MOEF) to provide technical and 
financial assistance to th e State governments. Such assistance may include; 
strengthening of infrastructure, sup port state-specific pr oject, organizing 
training programmes, etc. 
• Financial assistance to States/UTs on setting up of mode l facilities for 
demonstrating implementation of m unicipal solid waste Rules. Such 
assistance could be on the same lines  as has been done under NRCP and 
CETP schemes. 
•  Regular interaction meetings of co ncerned Ministries to up-date on the 
schemes formulated by them on solid waste management for local Bodies/ 
State Governments. 
• Convene interactive meetings with the local bodies of Metro cities and State 
Capitals along with concerned SPCBs for formulation of action plan for 
management of municipal solid waste. 
 
 
12    Thereafter, the matter was taken up for discussion with the representatives 
of the Department of Environmen t & Forests at Mumbai on the 8 th 
November, 2002. A study note was prepared. (Annexure VI). 
 
13    During the discussions the Committee was apprised that the said rules 
were under implementation. On Rule  4(2) regarding implementation 

 14
schedule, the representatives of th e State suggested for extension of 
deadline for providing suitable land  filling sites beyond December, 2003. 
On Rules 5 & 6 regarding inspection, the Committee reiterated its earlier 
suggestion that periodicity of inspectio n should be prescrib ed in the rules 
itself. The Committee also desired that  the Ministry should prescribe the 
manner in which a citizen could file a complaint, procedure of enquiry and 
the timeframe for completing the enquir y. On Rule 6(4) regarding period of 
authorization, the Committee had sugge sted that validity period of 
authorization should be prescribed at the earliest as time frame was a crucial 
aspect in this regard. On Rule 5 regarding criteria for complaints, it was 
suggested to the Committee that the local bodies should be provided with 
more powers as the existing State laws  were not effective. It was also 
suggested that strict punishment/penalty may be prescribed for the 
defaulting citizen. On schedule IV re garding terms and conditions of the 
agreement, the Committee was informed that due to variation in technology 
for treatment and disposal  of waste, it would not be possible to lay down 
terms and conditions governing the agreement. However, a draft agreement, 
indicating items to be negotiated, has been finalized. There was also an 
emphasis on proper equipment/technology and proper training as well. 
 
14      The Committee’s apprehensions regarding the efficacy of these Rules 
were confirmed during the meeting at Mumbai.  The representatives of the 
State Government sought more powers to the State Government and 
Municipal Corporations/Councils. Th ey sought waiver/relaxation in 
Customs Duty on the import of equipments. The Committee was informed 
that an amount of Rs 50 to 100 cr ores was required for the smooth 
implementation of the rules. The State representatives also asked for the 
subsidy from the Central Government as they were conve rting waste into 
bio-friendly manure whic h required huge capita l investment/support to 
make the project cost effective. The Committee was informed that there was 

 15
lack of adequate land filling sites in Mumbai and nearby. As a result the 
implementation of Rules was not up to th e mark. It was also informed that 
identified site is often subjected to  litigation. Regarding the implementation 
of Rule 7 pertaining to management of  municipal solid waste in compliance 
with the Schedules II, III and IV, the Committee asked the State 
Government to look into the suggestion that local bodies should be provided 
with more powers as the State Laws were not effective.  
 
15    Subsequently the Committee proceeded on its study visit to 
Bhubaneshwar on the 11
th November, 2002. The Study note was prepared 
(Annexure VII). 
 
16    During its interactions with the Committee, the representatives of 
Government of Orissa conveyed that they faced constraints pertaining to 
finances, lack of suitable and adequate landfill sites, time consuming 
process of acquisition of land, inad equate technical and managerial 
expertise. They proposed to seek priv ate participation, scope for resource 
generation and involve Dist rict Collectors. They also suggested that there 
was a need for financial support from the Centre and subsidy to the local 
bodies for the implementation of the Rules. However, the representative of 
the Union Ministry of Environment and Forest informed the Committee that 
the Central Government did not propos e any direct subsidy to the local 
bodies for the creation of facilities for treatment and disposal of municipal 
solid waste though the Central Government had provided adequate financial 
support for sensitization. In view of such constraints the State Government 
suggested the extension of deadline for suitable landfill sites. Regarding the 
Rule 7 pertaining to compliance, th e Committee was told that punitive 
provisions of the Environm ent (Protection) Act, 1986 would also apply to 
any non-compliance under these Rules. 
 

 16
17     Thereafter, the Committee took up the subject matter for discussion with 
the representatives of the State Government of Tamil Nadu and Andaman & 
Nicobar Islands Administration and the Ministry of Environment & Forests 
at Chennai on 28th January, 2003 and at Port Blair on 29 th January, 2003. A 
background note was provided on the issue. (Annexure VIII).  
 
18     Regarding Implementation Sc hedule Rule 4(2), the Committee was 
informed that the compliance of the implementation schedule was not likely 
to be achieved and it was suggested that dead-line for providing land filling 
sites as well as providing  disposal facilities should be extended beyond the 
December, 2003 dead-line. For th e Andaman & Nicobar Islands 
Administration, disposal of plastic wa ste was posing a serious problem and 
they suggested that plastic waste may be re exported. Another problem was 
disposal of saw dust. In the Andaman and Nicobar, Port Blair was the only 
urbanized pocket with a Municipal Counc il. It was informed that of 85 
metric tones of solid waste generated every day, only 65 metric tones could 
be collected and transported to disposal site which was  13 Km away from 
Port Blair.  The Committee noted that  the Ministry of Environment and 
Forest were providing financial assistance to the Andaman Pollution 
Control Committee.  
 
19     As regards the progress made in implementation of these Rules in Tamil 
Nadu, the Committee noted that efforts have been made to sensitise the 
local bodies and administration of the provisions made in the Rules. The 
Department of Municipal Administration of the State Government has been 
regularly interacting w ith the municipal loca l bodies and district 
administration. The Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board has conducted 
workshops on ‘Towards Zero garbage’  for stakeholders. The Committee 
was informed that under Section 5 of  the Environment (Protection) Act, 

 17
1986, the Tamil Nadu Pollution Contro l Board had issued notice and 
direction to the local bodies against whom it received complaints. 
 
20     The Committee then discussed the matter with the representatives of the 
State Government of Gujarat and the Mi nistry of Environment & Forests at 
Ahmedabad on 1st July, 2003. The study note on the said visit was prepared 
(Annexure IX). 
 
21    The representative of the Governme nt of Gujarat informed that regarding 
‘overall responsibil ity for the enforcement of rules as per Rule 5, the 
Secretary, Urban Development and Urban Housing Development was 
responsible for the enforcement of Ru les in Municipal Corporations and 
that the District Magistrates were over all responsible in respect of 
Municipalities. It was conveyed that the State Government accordingly 
proposed an amendment to the Rule 5.  
 
22     The Committee was informed that the main hurdles in implementation of 
the Rules by the Urban Local Bodies  (ULB) in the St ate was lack of 
financial resources with the ULBs. The State Government accordingly 
recommended amendments in the Rules/Sc hedules to facilitate their phased 
implementation starting from the bigge r municipalities. The norms for the 
smaller cities should be relaxed c onsidering their limited resources. The 
amendments to the Municipal Solid Wastes (Management and Handling) 
Rules, 2000 as proposed by the State Government of Gujrat is enclosed as 
(Annexure X) 
 
23     In the light of the discussions held with the State Governments along 
with the Ministry of Environment & Forests, the matter was pursued with 
the Ministry of Environment & Forest s. After a couple of reminders, the 
Ministry furnished their replies on 24
th April, 2007 (Annexure XI). 

 18
 
24    From the replies the Committee wa s informed that the Government had 
constituted a Committee to recommend amendments to the Rules including 
the modification in the Schedule I re garding the compliance of the Rules 
and to provide the periodicity of inspections under Rules 5 and 6.. It was 
also informed of the proposal to include punitive provisions under the 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, upon non-compliance of Rules.  The 
Committee observed distinct disjoint in the stands taken by the Center and 
the State Governments on operational issues.  
 
25     Considering the specific requirem ents of the solid waste management in 
the urban centers in hill areas, the Committee decided to hear the 
representatives of the Ministry of Environment & Forests, State 
Government of Himachal Pradesh and Municipal authorities of Shimla and 
Manali on 12
th June, 2009 and 16 th June, 2009, respectively. Study notes 
were prepared on the discussions at the two places. (Annexures XII and 
XIII). 
 
26      The Schedule III of the Rules has specific provision for the hilly areas. It 
has been provided that the municipal au thorities in such areas shall set up 
processing facilities for utilization of  biodegradable organic waste. The 
inert and non-degradable waste shall be  used in building roads or filling up 
appropriate areas on the hi lls. Because of constrai nts in finding adequate 
land in hilly areas, waste not suitable fo r road laying or filling up shall be 
disposed off in specially designed landfills.  
 
27      The Committee was informed that  the State Government had put a ban 
on the usage of plastic bags. A project  to use polythene waste in cement 
kilns was under submission to the Central Pollution Control Board. Further 
four roads have been identified by the PWD for the use of plastic waste in 

 19
road construction. The project propos al in this respect was under 
submission for financial assistance.  
 
28     The Committee was informed that in Himachal Pradesh only Shimla was 
covered under the JNNURM. Further entire  land in State was classified as 
forest, therefore as per the Forest Conservation Act, it can not be put to any 
non-forest use. As such the urban areas  were finding it difficult to dispose 
off non-bio-degradable urban waste, hence there was a problem of illegal 
dumping of urban debris in forest area.   
 
29     The Committee noted the demand to  cover more municipalities under 
JNNURM. The massive tourist influx imposed greater burden on the fragile 
ecology of the hilly State. The Committ ee noted that municipalities and the 
State Government faced financial constr aints and technological handicap in 
managing and processing the munici pal waste without disturbing the 
ecology.  
 
30     The Ministry of Environment a nd Forest informed the Committee that 
out of 56 municipalities, 41 were given authorizati on for setting up 
municipal solid waste management fac ility. However, none of those have 
been developed.  
 
31    As for the financial constraint faced by the municipalities, the Committee 
was informed that the Twelfth Finance Commission recommended 
devolution of grants of Rs. 5000 cror es to the Urban Local bodies during 
the period of 2005-2010 out of which half i.e. Rs 2500 crores was to be 
devolved exclusively for management  of municipal solid waste in 
accordance with these Rules.   
 

 20
32    Upon inquiring about the amendm ents that were supposed to be 
recommended by the Committee set up by the Ministry of Environment and 
Forest in 2007, the Ministry in its reply of the 4th November 2009, informed 
that the proposed amendments were still in the Draft Stage.  
 
 
General observation and recommendations of the Committee
 
 
33 Considering the tardy implementation of Rules and having analysed the relevant 
inputs and interactions with the Union Mini stry of Environment and Forest and the 
representatives of the select State G overnments, the Committee observes the 
following: 
 
34 The Committee, though in broad ag reement with the objectives of the 
Rules, considers that these Rules are no t in keeping with our Constitutional 
Scheme. The solid waste management is  included in Twelfth Schedule to the 
Constitution and Article 243W, empowers  the State Legislatures to frame 
legislations in respect of subjects incl uded in Twelfth Schedule. As such waste 
management is the primary responsib ility of the Municipal corporations/ 
Municipalities. 
 
35 The Committee also noted with concern that the State laws in respect of 
solid waste management were neither adeq uate nor effective.  The Committee 
is also aware of the financial and t echnological constraints faced by the 
Municipalities in implementing these Ru les, as was submitted by most of the 
State Governments before the Committee. 
 
36. The Committee also recognizes that the Union Government has framed 
these Rules under Section 3 of the Envi ronment ( Protection) Act, 1986, which 
bestows upon it sweeping powers to “ take  all such measures as is necessary or 
expedient for the purposes of prot ecting and improving the quality of 
environment and preventing, contro lling and abating environmental 
pollution”.  
 
37 During the meetings, the representa tives of the Central Government, 
however,  expressed inability for reaso ns not known to the Committee, to 
provide financial support or subsidy to the municipalities for the purposes of 
these Rules.  
 

 21
38 The Committee is at a loss to find a situation where the states/municipalities 
are required to implement Rules made  by the Central Government but 
without necessary financial, physical a nd technical support, which, as we all 
know, they can ill-afford. In such a scenario, the position of solid waste 
management in the country is pa thetic.  The Committee therefore, 
recommends that the Central Government should engage the State 
Governments and municipalities to a ddress the issue of funding through a 
mutually agreed institutionalised mechanism.  
 
39 The Committee is also of the view th at the Rules prescribe a complex and 
disjointed system of monitoring at District, State and Central levels. The 
elected bodies like municipalities are made accountable to Central and State 
Governments and the collateral authorit y like District Magistrate/Deputy 
Commissioner. As such the above structure is top heavy where single 
implementing agency is supposed to implement the rules without much 
resources and is accountable to layers of monitoring agencies. Such inverted 
system is perilous for the implementati on. The rules have identified District 
Magistrate/Deputy Commissioner as res ponsible for the implementation, 
without providing for delegation of power. The Committee wonders if the 
DM/DC beyond their routine revenue/administrative duties can monitor the 
implementation. Committee’s apprehensi ons are justified by the state of 
affairs in the Districts.   
 
40 The lack of earnestness in implementati on is reflected in the fact that the 
municipalities have repeatedly missed the deadlines as prescribed in Schedule 
I of the Rules. The Committee has been  informed that the Government now 
proposes to amend the Schedule I to extend the deadline till 2012. The 
Committee finds it unacceptable that the Rules framed in the year 2000 would 
not be implemented till 2012. The Committee recommends that the 
Government must take all the necessary measures as prescribed in Section 3 of 
the parent Act, to ensure that the proposed deadline of 2012 is not missed 
 
41 The Committee notes that the Ministry had prepared an Action Plan for 
the phase-wise implementation of these Rules. However, the Rules themselves 
did not provide for such phased implementation. The Action Plan also provide 
for a complex network of advisory and regulatory structure at the State and 
Centre levels which is extraneous to what has been provided in the Rules.
  
.  
 
42 The Committee also acknowledges that wi th the urbanization, it is difficult 
to find landfill sites for ever increasing volumes of solid waste. It has to be 
appreciated by the concern ed Governments that in  the interest of public 
health, such landfill sites should be loca ted at distant isolated places. However 
, the experience shows that with time urban settlement expands up to these 

 22
landfill sites. The existing Rules must provide for a safe buffer between such 
land fill sites and the human settlement . The Committee also feels that it is 
equally important that the facility of  composting and reprocessing of waste 
should be concurrently developed so as to evacuate the landfill sites. 
 
43 The Committee also recommends that the solid waste management and 
reprocessing should be an integral part of the present and future urban 
development and renewal schemes and programmes. And the finances out of 
these schemes/programmes should be de volved to the municipalities to fund 
the solid waste management and reprocessing.  
 
44 The solid waste management and re processing would require capital 
intensive technology. Going by the current status, the Committee is dissatisfied 
with the performance of Central Polluti on Control Board and State Pollution 
Control Boards, that were supposed to  provide technical support to the 
municipalities. The Committee recomme nds that the CPCB should present 
annual status report regarding implementation of Rules, to the Parliament. 
 
45 The Committee made an appraisal of the Action Plan prescribed by the 
Ministry of Environment and Forest a nd the amendments suggested by the 
Government of Gujrat. However, the Committee noted that these pragmatic 
suggestions have not been included in the Draft Amendment Rules. 
 
46 The Committee recommends that the ex perience of last ten years in the 
implementation of the Rules should be reflected in the proposed amendments. 
As such the financial, administrative and technical constraints faced by the 
State Government should be addressed in the amendments. 
 
47 The Committee recommends that the Government consider the above 
observations made by the Committee to  incorporate the same in the Draft 
Amendment Rules, it proposes to bring.

2. During the course of scrutiny of these Orders, the Committee has noted 
some cases where there has been a cons iderable time lag between the date of 
notification of the Order a nd the date of its laying. The annexed statement also

the schedule prescribed by the Committee and where such notifications were 
accompanied by a statement indicating the reasons for the delay in laying. In 
some of the cases the dela y has been quite long. The 
observations/recommendations of the Co mmittee in respect of the specific 
Ministries/Departments are as follows: -    
  
(i) Ministry of Agriculture (Depar tment of Agriculture Research and 
Education) 
  
 The Ministry of Agriculture (Depar tment of Agriculture Research and 
Education) have laid 4 notif ications with delay of 10 m onths in each case. All of 
them have been accompanied with delay statements. The reason for delay given 
by the Ministry is that the time taken to  get sufficient number of copies printed 
caused delay. 
  
 The Committee finds that the reply given by the Ministry as to the 
reasons of delay is not convincing and  appears to be evasive. Delay could be 
avoided, had precaution been taken by the Ministry in this regard. The 
Committee hopes that the Ministry of Ag riculture  would cut on such delays 
in future particularly on account of delay in receiving printed copies of 
notifications by evolving an effectiv e mechanism and would adhere to the 
time schedule as prescribed in Committee’s 131
st Report. 
 
(ii) Ministry of Commerce and Industry (Department of Commerce)  
 
The Department of Commerce have laid  five notifications out of which 
two notification (Sl. No. 26-27) have b een delayed. Delay period extends upto 5 
months and 8 months respectively.  There is no delay statement  appended with 
either of the notifications delayed. 
  
 The Committee emphasises that the Ministry of Commerce and 
Industry (Department of Commerce), strict ly adhere to the time schedule as 
recommended by it in its 131 st Report  in laying of the Subordinate 
Legislation before Parliament and in case of any delay in laying of the 
notifications, a delay statement sh ould also invariably be appended 
therewith. 
 
 

 
 
(iii) Ministry of Communicati on and Information Technology 
 
Ministry of Communication and Info rmation Technology have laid 7 
notifications and there is de lay in case of 1 notificat ion (Sl. No. 37) which has 
been delayed by 10 months. There is no delay statement  appended with it. 
 
The Committee is of the strong  views that the Ministry of 
Communication and Information Technol ogy  should take appropriate steps 
to prevent any delay in future for laying of Notifications on the table of the  
House and append delay statements where there has been a delay in laying of 
the notifications. 
 
(iv) Ministry of Consumer Affairs,  Food and Public Distribution  
 
(Department of Consumer Affairs) & (Department of Food and Public 
Distribution) 
 
Department of Consumer Affairs have laid four notifications two of which 
have been delayed. The delay period range s from four to six months. Department 
of Food and Public Distribution  have laid  fourteen notifications out of which two 
notifications (Sl. No. 57 & 58) have been delayed by five and nine months. There 
is no delay statement  appended with any of them. 
 
 The Committee is not happy over the delay in laying of notifications. 
Moreover there is no delay statem ent attached thereto. The Committee 
reiterates its recommendation that in case of delay in laying, notifications 
should invariably be accompanied with delay statement. The Ministry should 
take care that repetition of such delay is avoided in future.  
 
(v) Ministry of Corporate Affairs 
 
  Ministry of Corporate Affairs have laid 27 notifications out of which  11 
notifications (Sl. Nos. 71-74, 76-78, 85-87 & 89) have been delayed. Delay period

accompanied with delay statements and tw o notifications have  delay period of

 “The provisions of the Company Secretaries (Amendment) Act, 2006,

st March, 2006, 2007 and 2008. Therefor e the notifications could

 Ministry of Environment and Forest  have laid 29 notifications. Out of

 The Committee hopes that the Minist ry would avoid such instances of

 The Committee would like the Ministry of Finance (Department of

 The Committee would like to imp ress upon the Ministry of Finance

(Department of Ayush) 
 
 The Ministry of Health & Family We lfare (Department of Ayush) have 
laid 2 notifications out of which 1 has been delayed by seven month and  no delay
